meta.title: Hermeneutic of ecclesial continuity
meta.notice: This is a research layer written for this site. It applies a published method to disputed texts and records where the method succeeds, where it fails and where the evidence is not yet in. Its verdicts, confidence levels and the proposed synthesis on Constance, Basel and Vatican I are scholarly hypotheses, not teaching of the Catholic Church and not a judgment of any office of the Holy See.
plain: A text of the Church can be truly binding and still not be permanent. A law, a penalty, a pastoral rule or a prudential judgment binds while it is in force, and competent authority can later change it, because it was a determination for a time and a set of circumstances.

A definition is different. What the Church has proposed definitively cannot later be denied in the same sense. So the first question about any apparent reversal is what kind of act each text is, and what exactly it proposed.

Two texts conflict only if they say opposite things about the same subject, in the same sense, at the same time and in the same circumstances. Often they do not; sometimes they do. Where a real conflict remains after honest reading, this site says so instead of explaining it away.

Non-definitive teaching asks religious submission of mind and will, and the Church herself says such teaching can contain deficiencies (Donum Veritatis 24). How far divine assistance protects it is a theological question, which this site treats as open.
evidence_review: Record the witness and how it is known. Distinguish the enacted text, contemporary testimony, a draft, a later interpretation and a citation still to verify.

State the claim the evidence supports or weakens. For a contested legal act distinguish the fact of the act, the competence to perform it and the scope of its reception. If an act was revoked as a precaution, establish its prior force independently.
Compare the strongest rival explanations against the same evidence. Record the missing premise and what evidence could change the conclusion.
Rerun the conditions and comparisons. If the method itself changes, give the reason and retain the previous assessment alongside the new one.

formal_object.revealed: Revealed doctrine: proposed as divinely revealed.
formal_object.definitive: Definitive doctrine: proposed to be held definitively, connected with revelation.
formal_object.juridical: Juridical norm: a law, statute or canonical rule.
formal_object.moral_application: Moral application of a principle to circumstances.
formal_object.judicial: Judicial sentence: a judgment on persons or a case.
formal_object.dogmatic_fact: Dogmatic fact: a fact so connected with doctrine that the Church judges it.
formal_object.disputed: Disputed: what kind of claim this is, is itself the question.

assent.religious_submission: Religious submission of mind and will (canon 752; Lumen Gentium 25).
assent.obedience: Legal obedience to a law or precept while it is in force.
assent.prudential_deference: Respect and deference to a prudential judgment; reasoned disagreement possible.
assent.none: No assent is owed: a private opinion, a witness or a historical record.
assent.disputed: The grade of assent is itself disputed.

binding_status.not_juridical: Not a juridical act: legal force does not apply.
binding_status.in_force: A law or act in force now.
binding_status.lapsed: Was in force; has lapsed by disuse, fulfilment or change of circumstance.
binding_status.abrogated: Was in force; revoked or replaced by competent authority.
binding_status.annulled: Declared null from the start by competent authority.
binding_status.never_in_force: Never had legal force (no competent authority).
binding_status.disputed: Whether and how it bound is disputed.

evidence.H: Documented historical fact, with a source.
evidence.T: Defensible theological interpretation, held by recognised theologians.
evidence.N: Novel theory proposed on this site.
evidence.U: Unresolved claim: the evidence is not yet in or does not decide it.

verdict.demonstrated_concord: Demonstrated concord: every critical premise verified.
verdict.plausible_concord: Plausible concord: a substantial case, with a live objection.
verdict.unresolved_tension: Unresolved tension: the method has not reconciled the texts, or the research is incomplete.
verdict.textual_conflict_requires_revision: Textual conflict: the texts conflict as they stand; a reading or a classification must be revised.
verdict.not_comparable: Not comparable: different genre or subject.

matrix_result.apparent: Apparent conflict, removed by the reading given.
matrix_result.potential_contradiction: Potential contradiction: conflict if both are read in the sense stated.

stages: Open the complete primary text; verify the original language and, where possible, a critical edition; record citation and provenance.
Extract atomic propositions, with their qualifications and the text of any censure or condition.
Identify authority, genre, formal object, jurisdiction, grade of assent and binding status, each separately.
Record the controversy, tacit assumptions, confirmation, reception, later substitution or repeal, and current debate.
State rival propositions in identical logical terms (subject, quantifier, modality, time, circumstance) in a contradiction matrix.
Ask whether a legitimate determination, changed facts or different qualifications explain the change. Not an escape for opposite immutable moral claims.
Distinguish explanation and qualification from reversal; name the definitive content that survives.
For pope and council conflicts, apply the seven pass conditions; otherwise record "not applicable".
State the strongest evidence-based objection, with citations, and a fair rebuttal, or admit failure.
Confidence, evidence gaps, unanswered objections and the next most probative source.
A reader's summary, the detailed research, the opposing view, citations and labels for hypotheses.

benedict.source: Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia, 22 December 2005
benedict.status: An address, not a magisterial definition. It is used here as the method, not as a ruling on any of the cases below.
benedict.summary: Benedict XVI asked why the reception of the Second Vatican Council had been so hard, and answered that two hermeneutics had been at odds. A hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture reads the Council as a break, and looks for its true "spirit" beyond its texts, as if a council were a constituent assembly that could give the Church a new constitution. A hermeneutic of reform, of renewal in the continuity of the one subject Church, reads the Council as the same Church, growing and developing while remaining the same. Taking religious liberty as his example, he said that in the Church's concrete decisions on contingent matters there can be discontinuity, while continuity remains at the level of principle; recognising this is part of true reform.

rules.title: One enduring ecclesial subject
rules.text: No council is a constituent assembly empowered to replace the divinely given constitution of the Church.

rules.title: Separate principles from contingent expressions
rules.text: The same principle may generate different determinations under genuinely changed historical and juridical conditions.

rules.title: Permit correction of historical decisions
rules.text: Authentic reform may revise earlier concrete decisions without reversing the principles that motivated them.

rules.title: Prove continuity at the correct level
rules.text: Name the principle that actually continues; repeating the words "continuity" or "development" proves nothing.

rules.title: Respect the textual form
rules.text: The "spirit" of a document cannot override what the document says; an alleged historical qualification needs evidence.

benedict.inference_note: Where a case below applies these rules to Constance, Basel, the Jansenist condemnations or any other dispute, the application is this site's inference from Benedict's method, not his judgment on that dispute. He gave one worked example, religious liberty (case B1).

principles.title: Logical and propositional precision
principles.rule: Extract the exact subject, predicate, scope, modal force, qualifications, time and object of each claim. P and not-P conflict only when asserted in the same sense and circumstances; two time-bounded commands can differ without asserting contradictory universal doctrines.
principles.guards: Treating two texts as contradictory because their words clash, before their subjects, scopes and times are compared.

principles.title: Documentary priority and competence
principles.rule: Identify original language, critical text, date, promulgator, session, procedural status, confirmation, reception and repeal. Inclusion in Denzinger or omission from it is editorial evidence, not a doctrinal ruling.
principles.guards: Arguing from a translation, a summary or an editor's selection as if it were the act itself.

principles.title: Formal-object differentiation
principles.rule: Tag each claim as revealed doctrine, definitive doctrine, authentic non-definitive teaching, juridical norm, pastoral determination, moral application, judicial sentence, dogmatic fact, historical assertion or private opinion. One act can mix several.
principles.guards: Giving a whole document the weight of its weightiest sentence, or of its lightest.

principles.title: Proportionate assent and obligation
principles.rule: Distinguish divine and Catholic faith, definitive assent, religious submission of mind and will, legal obedience and prudential deference. Binding force, factual correctness, doctrinal truth and irreformability are four different properties.
principles.guards: Concluding from "this bound" that "this is irreformable", or from "this was changed" that "this never bound".

principles.title: Contingent determination under permanent authority
principles.rule: The divinely instituted power to bind and loose can ground real obligations that are neither uniquely best nor permanent (Aquinas's determinatio, applied by analogy). No human law can abrogate divine law. The analogy of an executive order illuminates governance, not the truth of competing doctrinal propositions.
principles.guards: Using "it was only discipline" to dissolve a claim the text proposes as true; or treating every law as an eternal truth.

principles.title: Homogeneous development
principles.rule: Show how a later clarification or qualification keeps the earlier definitive truth. Context must come from historical evidence; an exception may not be inserted simply because a contradiction would otherwise remain.
principles.guards: Calling any change "development", or any development "rupture".

principles.title: Indefectibility, infallibility and safety
principles.rule: Infallibility operates under defined conditions; indefectibility keeps the Church in the apostolic faith and constitution. A wider doctrinal safety (securitas doctrinalis) for non-definitive teaching is a theological theory, not a defined grade of the Magisterium. Donum Veritatis 23–31 admits limitations and deficiencies in prudential interventions.
principles.guards: Assuming that whatever was taught with authority must have been without error, or that whatever was not infallible may be ignored.

principles.title: Presumption of concord, with falsifiability
principles.rule: Seek a genuine historical reconciliation; state the best contrary interpretation; disclose any residual conflict. Never manufacture concord by reclassifying a plainly definitive claim as discipline or by leaving out difficult sentences. A failed or undetermined test stays visible.
principles.guards: Reaching the expected conclusion by changing the rules case by case.

levels.title: Logical
levels.test: Are the complete propositions truly P and not-P?

levels.title: Doctrinal
levels.test: Does later teaching preserve what was definitively taught?
levels.change: Formulation, development, clarification; not definitive negation.

levels.title: Juridical
levels.test: Was each rule valid during its own legal operation?

levels.title: Constitutional
levels.test: Does the one Church retain her divinely established offices?
levels.change: Extraordinary remedial arrangements, if independently justified.

gate.theory: Conditional extraordinary conciliar competence under a permanently Petrine constitution: a legitimately constituted general council might, under rigorously defined ecclesial emergencies, exercise a restorative competence immediately grounded in Christ, to protect the faith, to determine legitimacy in a schism, or to restore the lawful conditions of the Petrine office, without becoming a standing court superior to a certain and legitimate pope. This is novel and disputed; its existence and scope must be proved, not assumed.
conditions: Keep every definition of Vatican I intact.
Preserve real binding force for the early acts of Constance and Basel in their demonstrated sense.
Explain both the immediate, Christ-derived authority claimed and the resistance to papal dissolution.

Give an objective criterion for the emergency that a council could never invoke against a certain and peacefully accepted pope; show that the historical case met it under each rival account of which papal line was legitimate, and who convoked the council under each. A full procedure for future cases is not required.
Distinguish lawful amendment of contingent decrees from invalidation of their original authority.
Substantiate any limit placed on universal-sounding conciliar claims from their text and reception.
Answer a strong defender of Vatican I and a strong conciliarist without caricature.
gate.warning: Neither "Martin V confirmed everything" nor "Martin V rejected everything except individually confirmed acts" may be asserted as established fact without the exact text, a critical edition, a contextual reading and later corroboration. Omissions from Denzinger are not evidence of any office's judgment.
gate.rule: A failed condition means unresolved, not reconciled. D1 may never be marked demonstrated concord on the strength of a constitutional analogy alone.

history.text: Specify who discerns an emergency and who can convoke a legitimate council.
history.reason: Reworded in v0.3. The v0.2 wording asked the hypothesis for a working procedure for future emergencies. No received Catholic doctrine of an extraordinary case has one: the classical theologians never settled who declares a pope a heretic (Cajetan, Bellarmine, Suárez, John of St Thomas differ), and that doctrine is not thereby held incoherent. Requiring it of this hypothesis alone would break adversarial test 7. The condition keeps its purpose: without an objective criterion, any council could claim an emergency against a certain pope, which would rebuild the standing tribunal that condition 1 excludes. The v0.3 wording also requires the historical case to be tested under each rival account of the legitimate papal line. Disclosure: the rewording was made after D1 had failed under v0.2, and it can change D1's verdict; both verdicts are shown.

adversarial: Do we preserve the strongest wording of the earlier source?
Have we identified a principle that really continues, rather than inventing one?
Are later terms being read anachronistically into an earlier text?
Does "context" improperly convert universal moral teaching into local policy?
Is the conclusion dependent on a disputed papal confirmation or quotation?
Can an opponent accurately restate our conclusion without conceding our premises?
Would the same rules yield an unfavourable conclusion for a text we favour?
Has the site distinguished historical research from teaching promulgated by the Church?

cases.title: Cum occasione: what the five propositions condemn
cases.question: Does a condemnation attach to the literal wording of a proposition, to its sense in the author's system, or to every possible orthodox construal of the words?
cases.summary: Innocent X condemned five propositions on grace in 1653, giving each its own censure. Some of their words resemble Augustine; the Jansenists said that the propositions, read in Augustine's sense of efficacious grace, were orthodox and not in Jansen. The texts answer the first question themselves: the censures are assigned one by one, and Alexander VII declared that they were condemned "in the sense understood by" Jansen. A sense that keeps the Thomist doctrine of efficacious grace, which Paul V had allowed, is not touched. The live question is only whether a given orthodox reading still says what the proposition says.

texts.label: Alexander VII, Ad sacram beati Petri sedem (16 October 1656)
Paul V on the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1607)

propositions.says: Proposition 1 (some commandments are impossible to the just who will and strive, the grace that would make them possible being lacking) is condemned as rash, impious, blasphemous and heretical.

propositions.quote: In the state of fallen nature one never resists interior grace
propositions.says: Proposition 2 (in fallen nature interior grace is never resisted) is condemned as heretical.

Proposition 5 (it is Semipelagian to say Christ died for all without exception) is condemned with graded notes: false, rash and scandalous, and heretical if understood to mean that Christ died only for the predestined.
propositions.note: The censure itself names a sense.

propositions.quote: in the sense understood by that same Cornelius condemned
propositions.says: The propositions are taken from Jansen's Augustinus and condemned in the sense he intended.
Paul V lets Thomists and Molinists each teach their account of efficacious grace and forbids either to call the other heretical.

matrix.why: Grace efficacious of itself (the Thomist thesis allowed in 1607) does not say that grace is never resisted: in that school sufficient grace is resisted, and the will moved by efficacious grace is free. Different predicates.
The censure of proposition 5 already distinguishes senses; Alexander VII adds which sense is the author's. Together they condemn a determinate sense, not every construal of the words.

cases.qualifications: Censures assigned to each proposition, not in globo; proposition 5 carries a conditional note of heresy.
cases.reception: The Jansenists accepted the condemnation of the propositions "in themselves" and denied that they were in Jansen (the droit/fait distinction); see case A2. Dominicans held that their doctrine of efficacious grace was untouched, and Rome did not contradict them.
cases.contingency: Not a contingent determination: a doctrinal condemnation. The test does not apply.
cases.development: What survives unchanged: grace can be resisted; the commandments are possible with grace; Christ died for all. Later teaching (Trent before, the Catechism after) is consistent with each.
cases.hypothesis: The condemnation attaches to each proposition in the sense its censure names and, by 1098, in the sense of Jansen's Augustinus. It does not attach to every sense the words could bear, and it leaves the schools free on how grace is efficacious. (T)
cases.objection: If the condemnation is only of "Jansen's sense", and that sense is said to be Augustine's on efficacious grace, the Church condemned Augustine, or else the condemned sense is so thin that nothing definite is condemned.
cases.rebuttal: The propositions are not Augustine's doctrine of efficacious grace: proposition 2 denies that grace is ever resisted, proposition 1 that the just always have the grace to keep the law. The Thomists held efficacious grace while affirming both, and Rome let them. The condemned sense is definite: grace never resisted, commandments impossible, Christ dying only for the elect.

cases.title: Ad sacram: the binding force of a dogmatic fact
cases.question: When Alexander VII declared that the five propositions are in Jansen's book and condemned in his sense, what kind of claim was that: a dogmatic fact, a historical fact, or a judgment derived from the first condemnation?
cases.summary: The Jansenists accepted the condemnation of the five propositions but denied that Jansen held them, and offered "respectful silence" on that question of fact. Alexander VII declared it as a fact, a formulary required subscription, and Clement XI ruled that silence does not satisfy the obedience owed. Theologians call such a judgment a dogmatic fact: a fact so tied to doctrine that the Church can judge it. The 1998 commentary on the Profession of Faith lists dogmatic facts among truths held definitively, though it does not name this one. The classification is the established theological reading; whether every particular dogmatic fact is infallibly judged is a further question that the texts do not settle.

texts.label: Alexander VII, the formulary of submission (1665)
Doctrine of the Faith, commentary on the Professio fidei (1998)

propositions.quote: have been taken from the book of the aforementioned Cornelius Jansen
propositions.says: The five propositions are taken from the Augustinus and condemned in Jansen's sense.
A formulary of submission to both constitutions, to be signed by clergy and religious.

propositions.quote: is not satisfied by any obsequious silence
propositions.says: The obedience owed is not satisfied by respectful silence; the condemned sense of Jansen's book must be rejected in heart.
Truths connected with revelation by historical necessity, such as dogmatic facts, belong to the second paragraph of the Profession: held definitively.
propositions.ext: Doctrine of the Faith, commentary on the Professio fidei, no. 11 (1998)

matrix.why: The 1998 commentary gives the class; Ad sacram is the classical instance. Whether this instance was judged infallibly is not stated by either text.
The formulary is a juridical instrument that has lapsed; the teaching that interior assent is owed to such a judgment does not depend on it.

cases.qualifications: Ad sacram defines "in the sense understood by" Jansen; Vineam Domini speaks of "the sense of that book".
cases.reception: Fénelon and the anti-Jansenist theologians defended the Church's competence over dogmatic facts; Arnauld and Pascal denied it. Modern manuals treat dogmatic facts as a secondary object of infallibility, a thesis theologians call common but not defined.
cases.contingency: The formulary was a disciplinary measure and has lapsed. The judgment of fact is not contingent in that way.
cases.development: The category was clarified, not changed, by the 1998 commentary.
cases.hypothesis: Ad sacram is a judgment of dogmatic fact, binding with definitive assent according to the common theological reading, and consistent with the 1998 commentary. (T)
cases.objection: Whether a sentence is in a book, and in what sense its author meant it, is a historical question that revelation does not contain. To demand interior assent to it is to extend the Church's protection beyond faith and morals (P7). Modern historians also argue that some propositions are not verbatim in the Augustinus.
cases.rebuttal: The judgment is not that the words occur verbatim but that the book teaches their sense; and the Church cannot guard a doctrine if it cannot say which books teach its contrary. That is the reason given for the secondary object. The objection stands against any claim that this particular judgment is defined dogma, which the site does not make.

cases.title: Unigenitus: how censures given in globo are distributed
cases.question: When 101 propositions are condemned together under a list of censures, which censure falls on which proposition, and what role does Quesnel's context play?
cases.summary: Clement XI condemned 101 propositions from Quesnel's Réflexions morales together, with a list of censures from "false" to "heretical", without saying which fits which. Some propositions are close to Augustine or Prosper. The censures given in globo mean that each proposition deserves at least one of the notes, not necessarily the gravest, and the condemned sense is the one each had in Quesnel's book and system. The Roman record shows the Pope himself hesitating over several near-patristic propositions, so the condemned sense has to be shown proposition by proposition, not assumed. The site already discusses this case in its guide to reading a condemnation.

texts.label: J. M. Gres-Gayer, "The Unigenitus of Clement XI: A Fresh Look at the Issues", Theological Studies 49 (1988) 259–82

propositions.says: Proposition 13: when God wills to save a soul and touches it with the interior hand of grace, no human will resists him.
propositions.note: Near-quotation of Augustine, De correptione et gratia; Clement suspended judgment on it (Gres-Gayer, p. 268).

propositions.says: All 101 propositions are condemned as respectively false, captious, scandalous, rash, erroneous, heretical and the rest, as they stand in the book.
Proposition 29: outside the Church no grace is granted.
propositions.note: The rejection of this proposition is used again in B3.

matrix.why: The in globo censure does not declare proposition 13 heretical; it says it deserves at least one note, which may be "captious" or "ill-sounding" in its setting. That removes the charge that Augustine was condemned, but leaves open which note applies.

cases.qualifications: Censures in globo and respectively; the propositions are condemned "as they stand" in Quesnel's book.
cases.reception: Appealed against by part of the French episcopate (the Appellants); made a law of the State in France in 1730; argued for decades. Gres-Gayer's study of the preparation shows the Pope's own doubts over propositions 12, 13, 23 and 33.
cases.contingency: Not applicable to the doctrinal censures. The French conflicts over the bull's civil enforcement were contingent and have lapsed.
cases.development: Nothing defined in the bull was later reversed. The rejection of proposition 29 is kept in later teaching on grace outside the visible Church (LG 16).
cases.hypothesis: Each proposition is condemned in the sense it had in Quesnel's work, under at least one of the listed notes. The bare words of a near-patristic proposition do not show that a Father was condemned. (T)
cases.objection: If the condemned sense of proposition 13 cannot be distinguished from Augustine's, then either Augustine was censured or the bull condemned nothing definite in it; the Pope's own hesitation suggests the first.
cases.rebuttal: The bull does not say which note fits proposition 13, and a light note such as "captious" can fall on true words used to carry a false thesis (irresistible grace as Quesnel's system meant it). That is a real but limited concession: the site keeps the case close, as Clement XI did.

gaps.what: Quesnel's text for each disputed proposition, in its setting
gaps.settles: The condemned sense of propositions 12, 13, 23 and 33.

cases.title: Auctorem fidei and Pistoia: the same proposal, judged differently
cases.question: Pius VI condemned the Synod of Pistoia's liturgical and pastoral proposals; the Church later adopted similar practices. Did the proposals change, or the judgment, or the reasons?
cases.summary: The Synod of Pistoia (1786) proposed, among much else, more use of the vernacular. Pius VI censured its proposition 66 "if understood" as requiring the vernacular in the liturgical prayers, with prudential notes: false, rash, disturbing to the prescribed order, likely to cause harm. Vatican II later allowed the vernacular. The censure attaches to a sense (that apostolic practice and God's plan require the vernacular) and to a prudential judgment in that setting; the later permission does not assert that sense. The pattern holds for several Pistoia propositions; the limbo proposition (26) is a different case, treated in D5.

propositions.quote: if understood to signify introducing of the use of popular language into the liturgical prayers
propositions.says: Proposition 66, understood as requiring the vernacular in the liturgy, is false, rash, disturbing to the prescribed order and likely to cause harm.
Trent anathematises the claim that Mass must be celebrated only in the vernacular.
Latin is to be preserved in the Latin rites; the vernacular may be given a wider place, as competent authority decides.
propositions.ext: Sacrosanctum Concilium 36

matrix.why: Pistoia: apostolic practice requires the vernacular. Vatican II: the vernacular may be used where authority judges it useful. A claim of necessity against a permission: different modality.
Trent condemns "only in the vernacular"; Sacrosanctum Concilium keeps Latin and permits the vernacular.

cases.qualifications: "If understood to signify"; censures of the prudential class.
cases.reception: Pistoia was received in Tuscany, then retracted under Leopold's successor; the bull was opposed by Gallican and Josephinist circles. Its liturgical censures were cited in the twentieth-century debates on the vernacular on both sides.
cases.contingency: Passes: the judgment that introducing the vernacular was imprudent in 1794 is a prudential determination; its reversal in 1963 under other conditions does not deny a doctrine.
cases.development: What survives: no rite is required in the vernacular by divine law, and the Church decides the language of her liturgy.
cases.hypothesis: The Pistoia censures that carry prudential notes condemn a sense (a claim of necessity) and a judgment of timeliness; later permission of the practice is a different proposition. (T)
cases.objection: The censure "false" is not merely prudential, and Pius VI plainly opposed the practice itself, not only a claim of its necessity; reading "if understood" as protecting the later practice is anachronistic.
cases.rebuttal: "False" attaches to the proposition as censured: that apostolic practice and the plans of God require the change. Opposing the practice in 1794 is the prudential part, and the notes "rash, disturbing, productive of evils" are notes about prudence. The objection is right that Pius VI would not have favoured the 1963 reform; it does not show that the reform asserts what he condemned.

gaps.what: The Latin of propositions 31–35 and 66 with their notes
gaps.source: Auctorem fidei in Bullarii Romani continuatio
gaps.settles: Whether the conditional clauses are rendered fully.

cases.next_source: The Latin of Auctorem fidei, proposition 66.

audio.taught: Pius VI censured the Synod of Pistoia's statement that apostolic practice and God's plan call for the people's own language in the liturgy.
audio.authority: A papal constitution, with censures of the prudential kind: false, rash, disturbing, harmful.
audio.permanence: Permanent: that the vernacular is not required by divine law. Contingent: whether to use it, which the Church later decided differently.

cases.title: Baius, Trent and concupiscence
cases.question: How do the condemnation of Baius, Trent's teaching on original sin, and later accounts of remaining concupiscence fit together, and what was left to the schools?
cases.summary: Trent taught that baptism takes away everything that has the true and proper nature of sin, and that the concupiscence that remains is called sin by Paul only because it comes from sin and inclines to it. Pius V condemned 79 propositions of Michael du Bay, among them that concupiscence is itself a sin or a transgression of the commandment, "respectively" and "in the strict and proper sense intended by" their authors, granting that some could be held in some sense. The two acts agree: Trent defined, Pius V condemned a system that contradicted it. What the schools may still dispute is how nature, grace and the state of integrity relate, and which of the 79 might bear an orthodox sense.

texts.label: Trent, session 5, decree on original sin (17 June 1546)
Pius V, Ex omnibus afflictionibus (1 October 1567)

propositions.quote: the whole of that which has the true and proper nature of sin is not taken away
propositions.says: Anathema to whoever says that baptism does not take away the whole of what has the true and proper nature of sin; concupiscence that remains is not sin properly so called.
Baius 74: concupiscence in the regenerate who fall back into mortal sin, and in whom it dominates, is a sin.
Baius 75: the bad impulses of concupiscence are forbidden by "Thou shalt not covet", so a man aware of them who does not consent transgresses the precept, though not sinfully.

propositions.quote: in the strict and proper sense intended by those asserting them
propositions.says: The propositions are condemned respectively, with notes from heretical to offensive, in their authors' sense; some could be maintained in some way.

matrix.why: Trent: remaining concupiscence is not sin properly speaking. Baius 75: unconsented impulses transgress a commandment. A transgression of a commandment of God is what Trent calls sin; the condemnation removes the conflict by rejecting Baius.

Which note falls on 74 is not said; read of habitual sin in the relapsed, it could bear a sense close to ordinary teaching on vicious habits. The famous "comma" in 1080 leaves unclear which clause the concession belongs to.

cases.qualifications: "Respectively"; "in the strict and proper sense intended"; "although some could be maintained in some way".
cases.reception: The placement of the comma in 1080 (the comma Pianum) was argued for a century; Louvain resisted; Gregory XIII renewed the bull. Augustinian and Thomist schools continued to dispute pure nature, which later Henri de Lubac's work reopened.
cases.contingency: Not applicable: doctrinal definitions and condemnations.
cases.development: Trent's doctrine stands unchanged in the Catechism (CCC 1264, 405).
cases.hypothesis: Trent defines; the bull condemns Baius's system in his sense with graded notes; the schools stay free on the nature–grace questions the bull does not decide. (T)
cases.objection: If some propositions "could be maintained in some way", the condemnation does not fix a doctrine for them; and later Augustinian theology, including de Lubac on the natural desire for God, comes close to propositions the bull condemned.
cases.rebuttal: The bull fixes which sense is condemned, the author's; it does not need to condemn every sense. Whether de Lubac's thesis reproduces a condemned sense was itself argued (Humani generis 26 warned against denying the gratuity of the supernatural); that is a live school dispute, not a reversal.

gaps.what: The Latin of 1080 with the disputed comma
gaps.source: The bull in Bullarium Romanum; Le Bachelet's study
gaps.settles: Which clause the concession qualifies.

cases.next_source: The Latin of Ex omnibus afflictionibus, closing clause.

audio.taught: Trent taught that baptism removes everything that is truly sin, and that the leftover inclination to sin is not itself sin. Pius V condemned propositions of Michael du Bay, including that this inclination is a sin or breaks a commandment.
audio.authority: Trent's canon is a definition. Pius V's bull condemns 79 propositions with graded censures, in the sense their authors meant.
audio.permanence: Permanent: Trent's teaching on original sin and concupiscence. Still open: how nature and grace relate, which the schools continue to argue.

cases.title: Quanta cura and the Syllabus beside Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Is the liberty Pius IX condemned the same proposition as the civil immunity from coercion that Dignitatis Humanae declares a right?
cases.summary: Gregory XVI called it "insanity" that liberty of conscience must be claimed for everyone, and Pius IX condemned the opinion that liberty of conscience and worship is each man's proper right, to be proclaimed in law in every well-ordered society. Vatican II declared that the human person has a right to religious freedom, an immunity from coercion within due limits, to be recognised in constitutional law. Benedict XVI used this as his example of reform in continuity: the condemnations rejected a liberty grounded in indifference to truth, the Council affirmed an immunity grounded in the dignity of the person, and the Council says it leaves the traditional doctrine on duties toward the true religion untouched. The case is substantial but contested; the words "proper right of every man ... proclaimed by law" come close to what the Council says.

texts.label: Pius IX, Quanta cura and the Syllabus (8 December 1864)
Benedict XVI, Address to the Roman Curia (22 December 2005)

propositions.quote: liberty of conscience and of worship is the proper right of every man, and should be proclaimed and asserted by law in every correctly established society
propositions.says: Condemned: that liberty of conscience and worship is every man's proper right, to be proclaimed in law, with a right to all manner of liberty unrestrained by any authority.
Syllabus 79, condemned: that civil liberty of every cult and full power to manifest any opinion does not lead more easily to corruption and indifferentism.

propositions.quote: liberty of conscience must be claimed and defended for anyone
propositions.says: Gregory XVI: from indifferentism flows the "insanity" that liberty of conscience must be claimed for anyone.

propositions.quote: the human person has a right to religious freedom
propositions.says: The person has a right to religious freedom: immunity from coercion by any human power, within due limits, founded in dignity, to be a civil right.
The Council leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of men and societies toward the true religion.
propositions.note: The sentence is in DH 1; check that the site's excerpt includes it.

matrix.why: Same predicate class ("right", "proclaimed by law"). Different grounds and objects: the condemned opinion grounds the right in a liberty unrestrained by any authority and joined to indifferentism; the Council grounds an immunity from coercion in the dignity of the person, within due limits of public order, and keeps the duty toward truth. Concord holds if the grounds and limits are part of the propositions; conflict if "right ... proclaimed by law" is the whole of each.
Syllabus 79 is a factual-prudential judgment (unlimited liberty leads more easily to corruption); the Council's immunity is limited by public order. Different predicates.

cases.qualifications: Quanta cura: the right "to all manner of liberty ... not to be restrained by either ecclesiastical or civil authority". Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits"; "leaves untouched traditional Catholic doctrine".
cases.reception: John Courtney Murray and the majority at the Council read development; Archbishop Lefebvre and later traditionalist critics read rupture; Thomas Pink reads the earlier texts as about the Church's jurisdiction over the baptised, which the Council does not address; Basile Valuet catalogues the readings. Benedict XVI (2005) presents it as reform in continuity.
cases.contingency: Partly: the confessional State and the toleration Leo XIII allowed (1874) were contingent arrangements. The test does not apply to the claim of a natural right, which is doctrinal.
cases.development: What survives: the duty to seek and embrace the truth; the rejection of indifferentism; the freedom of the act of faith from coercion (Trent and earlier). What is new: the explicit civil right.
cases.hypothesis: The nineteenth-century acts condemned a right grounded in indifference to truth and unrestrained by any authority; the Council declared an immunity grounded in dignity, limited by public order and joined to the duty toward truth. These are different propositions. (T)
cases.objection: "Liberty of conscience and of worship is the proper right of every man, and should be proclaimed and asserted by law" is almost word for word what Dignitatis Humanae 2 declares. The distinction of grounds is supplied by the interpreter, not by Pius IX, who also condemned the claim (Syllabus 77–78) that other cults should be admitted in Catholic countries.
cases.rebuttal: The condemned sentence continues: a right "to all manner of liberty ... not to be restrained by either ecclesiastical or civil authority", which the Council does not assert. Syllabus 77–78 concern the confessional State in particular circumstances, a contingent arrangement (P5). The objection keeps its force against any claim that nothing changed; the site claims development, not identity.

gaps.what: The full sentence of DH 1 on the traditional doctrine
gaps.settles: That b1-dh1 is quoted from the site's excerpt.

cases.next_source: The Latin of Quanta cura 3, to compare "ius proprium" with Dignitatis Humanae 2.
cases.benedict: Benedict XVI's own example: he names religious liberty as a case where contingent decisions changed while the principle continued. This case follows his judgment and is not an inference.

audio.taught: Pius IX condemned the idea that freedom of conscience and worship is everyone's right, to be written into law, with no authority able to limit it. The Second Vatican Council taught that everyone has a right not to be coerced in religion, within the limits of public order, and that this should be a civil right.
audio.authority: Papal encyclicals and the Syllabus on one side; a declaration of an ecumenical council on the other. Neither is a solemn definition.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the duty to seek the truth, and the freedom of the act of faith. Contingent: the confessional State. Disputed: whether the two texts speak of the same right.

cases.title: Lateran IV, canon 3, beside Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Does a once-legitimate penal law against heretics conflict with a later right to religious freedom grounded in human dignity?
cases.summary: Lateran IV's canon 3 required secular powers to expel heretics from their lands, under ecclesiastical penalties. Dignitatis Humanae teaches that no one may be coerced in religion by any human power, as a right founded in dignity. If the canon was a juridical determination that bound in its time, and the Council's right is a natural right, then the canon commanded something the Council says is contrary to a natural right. That is a tension at the moral level, not only a change of law. Two readings try to remove it, neither yet established. The site does not hold the penal clauses of canon 3, so the case is at an early stage.

texts.label: Lateran IV, constitution 3 (1215): the necessity of a canonical mission
texts.note: The site's excerpt gives only the clause on unauthorised preaching, not the penal clauses on heretics.

propositions.says: Secular authorities are to be admonished and if necessary compelled by censure to expel heretics; a ruler who neglects it may be excommunicated and his vassals released.
propositions.ext: Lateran IV, constitution 3, penal clauses (COD 233–235)

propositions.quote: That heretics be burned is against the will of the Spirit
propositions.says: Luther's proposition 33 is among those condemned respectively.
No one may be forced to act against his beliefs by any human power, within due limits; the right is founded in the dignity of the person.

matrix.why: A law against a declared right: if the law's content is coercion of religious acts that the right forbids, the law commanded what is unjust. Two readings: (1) the law concerned the baptised under the Church's jurisdiction, which the Council's civil right does not address (Pink); (2) the law was an erroneous application of principle in its time, reformable because not definitive. The first is unproved from the text; the second concedes a moral error in a conciliar law.
Proposition 33 is condemned in globo; it may deserve only a light note, and its condemned sense may be the denial that the Church may punish at all.

cases.qualifications: Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits"; it speaks of "any human power".
cases.reception: On the Day of Pardon (12 March 2000) John Paul II asked forgiveness for the use of violence in the service of truth. Pink argues for a jurisdictional reading; Murray for development; others for a reversal of a moral judgment.
cases.contingency: The law is plainly contingent and abrogated. The test does not reach the question whether it was ever just, which is a moral claim (stage 6 forbids using contingency as an escape here).
cases.development: Undetermined until the canon's text and the Council's scope are compared.
cases.hypothesis: Two candidate readings, neither established: jurisdiction over the baptised (Pink), or a fallible conciliar law whose moral premise the Church later corrected. (U)
cases.objection: A general council commanded rulers to coerce on religious grounds; if religious freedom is a natural right, the council commanded an injustice, and calling the canon "discipline" does not change what it commanded.
cases.rebuttal: None decisive. The site marks the case unresolved: the conciliar law bound as law in its time; whether it was morally just is a further question the Church has not settled by definition, and Donum Veritatis 24 allows that prudential interventions can be deficient.

gaps.what: The full text of Lateran IV, constitution 3
gaps.settles: What the canon commanded and to whom.

gaps.what: The scope of "any human power" in DH 2, from the relatio
gaps.settles: Whether the Council meant to include ecclesiastical penal power.

audio.taught: The Fourth Lateran Council told rulers to expel heretics from their lands, under Church penalties. The Second Vatican Council taught that no one may be forced in matters of religion by any human power.
audio.authority: A law of an ecumenical council, long since abrogated, and a conciliar declaration. Neither is a definition.
audio.permanence: The law was contingent and is gone. Whether it was just when it was made is the unresolved question: this site does not claim to have answered it.

cases.title: Outside the Church no salvation: Florence, Unam Sanctam and Lumen Gentium 14–16
cases.question: What do incorporation, desire, culpability and invincible ignorance mean in the teaching that there is no salvation outside the Church?
cases.summary: Florence taught that no one outside the Catholic Church, pagan, Jew, heretic or schismatic, can share in eternal life unless joined to her before death; Boniface VIII defined that subjection to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation. Pius IX taught that those in invincible ignorance of the true religion are not guilty for it before God. Lumen Gentium teaches that the Church is necessary, that those who know it and refuse to enter cannot be saved, and that those who through no fault do not know the Gospel can be saved by grace. The dogma stands in every text; what developed is the account of how a person is joined to the Church. The Holy Office letter of 1949 against Leonard Feeney's strict reading is not yet on the site.

texts.label: Pius IX, Singulari quadam (1854) and Quanto conficiamur (1863)
Holy Office, letter to the Archbishop of Boston (8 August 1949)

propositions.quote: those not living within the Catholic Church
propositions.says: Those not living within the Catholic Church cannot share in eternal life unless joined to her before death.
Unam Sanctam's closing sentence: it is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff.

propositions.quote: if this ignorance is invincible, are not stained by any guilt in this matter in the eyes of God
propositions.says: It is of faith that outside the Roman Church no one is saved; and it is certain that those in invincible ignorance are not guilty for it before God.

propositions.quote: would refuse to enter or to remain in it, could not be saved
propositions.says: Whoever, knowing that the Catholic Church was made necessary by Christ, would refuse to enter or remain, could not be saved.
Those who through no fault do not know the Gospel, but seek God and try to do his will, can attain salvation.

matrix.why: Florence names pagans and Jews among those who cannot be saved "unless joined" to the Church; Lumen Gentium 16 says some who do not know the Gospel can be saved. The conflict is removed if "joined" admits a union by grace and implicit desire (Pius IX, Pius XII, LG 16); it returns if Florence meant visible membership only, as Feeney read it, a reading the Holy Office rejected in 1949.
Both make culpability the condition: knowing refusal excludes, invincible ignorance does not incur guilt.

cases.qualifications: Florence: "unless before the end of life they are joined". Pius IX: "if this ignorance is invincible". Lumen Gentium 14: "knowing that". Lumen Gentium 16: "through no fault of their own".
cases.reception: The Feeney controversy (1949, excommunication 1953) fixed the rejection of the strictest reading. Some traditionalist theologians read Florence as requiring explicit faith; the common reading admits implicit desire.
cases.contingency: Not applicable: doctrine.
cases.development: What survives: the necessity of the Church and of faith and baptism; no salvation except through Christ. What developed: the account of how those outside visible membership are related to the Church.
cases.hypothesis: The dogma concerns the necessity of the Church, binding on all who know it; it does not define that every person not visibly a member is lost, which the Church has taught against since at least 1854. (T)
cases.objection: Florence names pagans, Jews, heretics and schismatics without qualification, and the Fathers it cites (Fulgentius) meant visible membership. "Joined" in the sense of Lumen Gentium is a later meaning read back into the text (adversarial test 3).
cases.rebuttal: Florence's own condition, "unless joined before death", leaves room for how; Trent had taught baptism of desire (n. 796), so the means were not limited to the visible rite even before 1854. The objection is strongest on the question how explicit faith must be, which remains open.

gaps.what: The Holy Office letter of 8 August 1949
gaps.settles: The authoritative rejection of the strict reading.

audio.taught: Florence taught that no one outside the Catholic Church can be saved unless joined to her before death. Pius IX and the Second Vatican Council taught that those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel can be saved by grace.
audio.authority: Florence and Boniface VIII define the necessity of the Church; Pius IX and Lumen Gentium are authoritative teaching on how it applies.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the Church is necessary for salvation, and salvation comes only through Christ. Developed: how people outside her visible boundaries can be joined to her.

cases.title: Cantate Domino, Nostra Aetate 4, and the covenant with Israel
cases.question: How do Florence's teaching on the ceremonies of the Law, Nostra Aetate 4 and later statements about the Jewish people and the covenant fit together?
cases.summary: Florence taught that the ceremonies of the Mosaic law ceased with Christ, and that after the promulgation of the Gospel they cannot be observed as necessary for salvation without mortal sin. Nostra Aetate 4 recalls the Church's bond with Abraham's stock, rejects the charge of deicide against the Jews as a people and deplores antisemitism; Lumen Gentium 16 and Evangelii Gaudium 247 speak of a covenant never revoked. Distinctions remove part of the tension: Florence speaks of observing the Law as necessary for salvation; the later texts speak of God's fidelity and of history, not of a separate way of salvation without Christ. Whether "never revoked" can be squared with Florence's "ceased" is not settled by these texts.

texts.label: Vatican II, Nostra Aetate 4 and Lumen Gentium 16
Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews, "The Gifts and the Calling of God are Irrevocable" (2015)

propositions.quote: placed hope in these matters of the law and submitted himself to them as necessary for salvation
propositions.says: The ceremonies of the Mosaic law ceased with Christ; whoever after the passion put hope in them as necessary for salvation sinned mortally; after the promulgation of the Gospel they cannot be observed without loss of eternal salvation.
The Church received the Old Testament through the people with whom God concluded the Ancient Covenant; the Jews are not to be presented as rejected or accursed.

propositions.quote: their covenant with God has never been revoked
propositions.says: The Jewish people's covenant with God has never been revoked.

matrix.why: Florence: the ceremonial law ceased as a way of worship and cannot be kept as necessary for salvation. Evangelii Gaudium: the covenant is not revoked. If "covenant" means God's election and promises (Rom 11:29), no conflict; if it means the Mosaic order of worship as salvific, conflict. Evangelii Gaudium cites Romans 11:29, which supports the first.
Nostra Aetate does not speak of observance of the Law as a means of salvation.

cases.qualifications: Florence: "as necessary for salvation"; "after the promulgation of the Gospel". Evangelii Gaudium: grounded in Romans 11:29.
cases.reception: The 2015 document of the Commission says the Church has no institutional mission to the Jews while holding that salvation is through Christ; critics on both sides read it as either too much or too little. Benedict XVI's 2018 article in Communio discussed "never revoked" and the "theory of substitution".
cases.contingency: Not applicable to the doctrine; the repudiation of antisemitism and of the deicide charge corrects historical attitudes and teaching (H).
cases.development: What survives: salvation through Christ alone; the ceremonial law fulfilled in him. What is clearer: God's fidelity to his election of Israel.
cases.hypothesis: Florence concerns the Mosaic ceremonies as a means of salvation; the later texts concern God's irrevocable election. No text teaches a separate salvific way without Christ. (T)
cases.objection: "Never revoked" in its natural sense denies the supersession Florence states ("ceased"), and the 2015 document's refusal of an institutional mission suggests in practice a separate way.
cases.rebuttal: The covenant language of Evangelii Gaudium rests on Romans 11:29, which Paul wrote while holding that the ceremonies do not justify. The concern about a separate way is about a commission document and practice, not about the conciliar or papal texts; it remains a live dispute.

gaps.what: The 2015 document, nos. 35–40
gaps.source: vatican.va, Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews
gaps.settles: Whether it asserts or denies a separate way.

audio.taught: Florence taught that the ceremonies of the Law of Moses ended with Christ and cannot be kept as necessary for salvation. The Second Vatican Council and Pope Francis taught that God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked, and rejected antisemitism.
audio.authority: A decree of an ecumenical council; a conciliar declaration; a papal exhortation.
audio.permanence: Permanent: salvation is through Christ; God keeps his promises. Unsettled: exactly what "covenant" means in each text.

cases.title: Mortalium animos and the 1927 decree beside Unitatis Redintegratio
cases.question: Does ecumenism imply the doctrinal indifferentism Pius XI condemned, or do different practices fall under one principle?
cases.summary: In 1927 the Holy Office forbade Catholics to take part in meetings that aimed to unite all who call themselves Christians on a single agreement, and Pius XI's Mortalium animos (1928) explained why: such meetings presumed that the Church of Christ does not yet exist and that unity is to be built out of the denominations, which is indifferentism. Vatican II's Unitatis Redintegratio encouraged Catholic participation in the ecumenical movement while warning against false irenicism and teaching a hierarchy of truths. The principle is the same, unity in the one Church and in the whole truth; the practice changed, and the Council explains why: the movement itself had changed, and Catholics were to take part without accepting its earlier premise.

texts.label: John Paul II, Ut Unum Sint (1995)

propositions.says: Catholics may not attend or take part in meetings of non-Catholics aiming to unite all who claim the name of Christian under a single agreement.
Such efforts presume that all religions or denominations are more or less good and that the Church of Christ is yet to be made; unity is return to the one true Church.
propositions.ext: Pius XI, Mortalium animos 2, 10

propositions.quote: in Catholic doctrine there exists a "hierarchy" of truths
propositions.says: Catholic theologians in dialogue stand fast by the Church's teaching; there is a hierarchy of truths; false irenicism is foreign to ecumenism.

matrix.why: A prohibition of participation in a particular kind of meeting, with a stated premise, against a permission to take part on Catholic principles. Different acts under the same principle.
Pius XI condemns indifferentism and the claim that the Church does not yet exist; the Council teaches that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church and rejects false irenicism.

cases.qualifications: The 1927 decree concerns meetings "which aim to associate together under a single agreement all who in any way lay claim to the name of Christian".
cases.reception: Traditionalist critics read a reversal of practice as a reversal of doctrine; the common reading is development of discipline under the same doctrine (Congar, Ratzinger).
cases.contingency: Passes: the prohibition was a prudential and juridical determination tied to the premises of the movements of the 1920s.
cases.development: What survives: the one Church; unity as communion in the whole faith; rejection of indifferentism.
cases.hypothesis: One principle (unity in the truth of the one Church), two determinations under different conditions. (T)
cases.objection: The ecumenical movement Catholics joined after 1964 is the same World Council lineage Pius XI refused, and its premise did not change; so the practice now presumes what Mortalium animos condemned.
cases.rebuttal: Unitatis Redintegratio states Catholic participation on Catholic premises (UR 3, 4, 11), and Dominus Iesus (2000) restated the doctrine that Pius XI defended. Whether every ecumenical practice keeps to that is a question of prudence, not of contradiction between the texts.

gaps.what: Mortalium animos, full text
gaps.settles: Its exact premises.

audio.taught: In 1927 and 1928 Rome forbade Catholics to join meetings that tried to build Christian unity by setting aside doctrinal differences. In 1964 the Second Vatican Council encouraged Catholics to take part in ecumenism, while holding to the whole of Catholic teaching.
audio.authority: A decree of the Holy Office and an encyclical; a conciliar decree.
audio.permanence: Permanent: unity in the one Church and the whole truth. Changed: the practical rule about taking part.

cases.title: Pastor aeternus and Lumen Gentium 22: collegiality and the primacy
cases.question: Is the episcopal college as a subject of supreme power consistent with the full Petrine jurisdiction Vatican I defined?
cases.summary: Vatican I defined that the pope has full and supreme jurisdiction over the whole Church, ordinary and immediate. Lumen Gentium 22 teaches that the order of bishops, together with its head and never without him, is also the subject of supreme and full power, which it cannot exercise without the pope's consent. The Preliminary Note of Explanation, added by Paul VI's order, says that the pope can always exercise his power freely and that the college never acts without its head. The texts were written to fit, and the Note is the authoritative key. The theological question of whether there are one or two subjects of supreme power remains open, but neither answer denies Vatican I.

texts.label: Vatican II, Lumen Gentium 22 and the Preliminary Note of Explanation

propositions.says: The Roman Pontiff has full and supreme, ordinary and immediate power of jurisdiction over the universal Church.
This power does not impede but asserts and strengthens the ordinary and immediate power of the bishops.
The order of bishops, with its head and never without him, is also the subject of supreme and full power over the universal Church, which it can exercise only with his consent.
"College" is not a group of equals; the pope can always exercise his power at will; the college does not act without its head.

matrix.why: Vatican I: the pope has full and supreme power. Lumen Gentium: the college with the pope has supreme power, exercised only with his consent. A second subject that includes the first and never acts without him does not limit him.

cases.qualifications: "Together with its head ... and never without this head"; "with the consent of the Roman Pontiff".
cases.reception: Rahner held one subject (the college with its head), the pope acting as its head; others hold two inadequately distinct subjects. Both are within the Note.
cases.contingency: Not applicable.
cases.development: Homogeneous: Vatican I's planned constitution on the Church was never finished; Lumen Gentium completes it.
cases.hypothesis: The two councils teach compatible propositions, and the Note fixes their relation. (D/T)
cases.objection: A college with supreme power, even with its head, is a second sovereign; Vatican I's "full" leaves no room for one.
cases.rebuttal: Vatican I itself says papal power "asserts, confirms and vindicates" episcopal power (n. 1828). A college that cannot act without the pope's consent takes nothing from fullness. The theoretical question of one or two subjects does not reach the definition.

gaps.what: The Latin of the Preliminary Note, n. 3–4
gaps.settles: The exact wording on the pope acting "ad placitum".

audio.taught: Vatican I defined that the pope has full and supreme authority over the whole Church. Vatican II taught that the bishops as a body, together with the pope and never without him, also have supreme authority.
audio.authority: A conciliar definition, and a dogmatic constitution with an explanatory note added by papal order.
audio.permanence: Permanent: both. What theologians still discuss is whether these are one subject of authority or two.

cases.title: Quas primas and Immortale Dei beside Dignitatis Humanae: the State and religion
cases.question: How do the duties of States toward the true religion, as Leo XIII and Pius XI taught them, relate to permissible constitutional forms and to civil religious liberty?
cases.summary: Leo XIII taught that the State, like individuals, owes worship to God and must not treat all religions alike, while allowing rulers to tolerate other worships for a great good or to avoid evil; Pius XI's Quas primas taught that Christ's kingship extends to civil society. Dignitatis Humanae teaches civil immunity from coercion and says it leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of societies toward the true religion. This case shares propositions with B1 and C5 and is linked to them rather than repeating them. Its own question is constitutional form: the earlier texts do not bind a State to a particular legal establishment, and the Council allows a special civil recognition of one religion.

texts.label: Leo XIII, Immortale Dei (1885) and Libertas (1888)

propositions.says: The Church does not condemn rulers who, for a great good or to prevent an evil, tolerate various forms of worship.
Christ as man has power over all civil affairs; whoever denies it errs gravely.
The Council leaves untouched the traditional doctrine on the moral duty of men and societies toward the true religion and the one Church of Christ.

matrix.why: A moral duty of societies toward the true religion, affirmed by both; no specific legal establishment is required by either.
Leo XIII: toleration as a permitted concession. The Council: immunity as a right. Treated in C5.

cases.qualifications: Immortale Dei: toleration "to obtain some great blessing or to prevent an evil". Dignitatis Humanae 6: special civil recognition of one community is permitted, provided religious freedom is respected.
cases.reception: Murray read the earlier texts as tied to the nineteenth-century confessional State; integralist writers read them as permanent doctrine of the confessional State. The post-conciliar concordats (Italy 1984, Spain 1979) dropped confessional clauses.
cases.contingency: Passes for the form of establishment, which is a contingent arrangement; not for the moral duty, which both affirm.
cases.development: What survives: the social kingship of Christ and the duty of societies toward the true religion. Changed: the legal forms the Church seeks.
cases.hypothesis: The duty is doctrinal; its legal expression is a determination under circumstances. (T)
cases.objection: If the State owes public worship to the true religion, it cannot also be bound to give every religion equal immunity; Dignitatis Humanae's "untouched" is a formula that conceals a change.
cases.rebuttal: Dignitatis Humanae requires immunity from coercion, not equal honour; it allows special recognition. The objection identifies a real pressure between the texts in their emphasis, which this site records in B1 and C5.

gaps.what: Dignitatis Humanae 6 on special civil recognition
gaps.settles: The Council's own allowance for establishment.

audio.taught: Leo XIII and Pius XI taught that societies, not only individuals, owe honour to God and to Christ the King, while rulers may tolerate other religions. The Second Vatican Council taught a civil right to religious freedom and said it leaves that duty untouched.
audio.authority: Encyclicals, and a conciliar declaration.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the duty of societies toward the truth. Contingent: the legal arrangement between Church and State.

cases.title: The death penalty: Innocent III, Evangelium Vitae and Catechism 2267 (2018)
cases.question: Does "inadmissible" in the revised Catechism 2267 name an intrinsic moral object, or a judgment about changed conditions and penal options?
cases.summary: In 1210 Innocent III required the Waldensians to accept that secular power may impose the death penalty without mortal sin, provided it acts in judgment, not hatred. John Paul II taught in 1995 that it should not go to that extreme except in cases of absolute necessity, which today are very rare if not non-existent. In 2018 the Catechism was revised to say that the death penalty "is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person". The revised text gives two kinds of reason: changes of fact (better systems of detention, a new understanding of penal sanctions) and the dignity of the person. If the first governs, the change is a prudential application and no definitive teaching is touched. If the second means the penalty is wrong in itself, it contradicts 1210. The text supports both readings, and so does the commentary on it; the site marks the case unresolved.

texts.label: Innocent III, profession of faith for the Waldensians (1208, clause added 1210)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2267, revised (1 August 2018)
Doctrine of the Faith, letter to the bishops on the revision (2 August 2018)

propositions.quote: without mortal sin it is possible to exercise a judgment of blood
propositions.says: Secular power can exercise a judgment of blood without mortal sin, if it punishes in judgment and not in hatred, advisedly and not rashly.
propositions.note: A clause in a profession imposed on returning Waldensians; its grade is disputed (definitive teaching on a moral matter, or an authentic statement in a particular profession).

propositions.quote: except in cases of absolute necessity
propositions.says: Punishment ought not go to the extreme of execution except in cases of absolute necessity, which today are very rare if not practically non-existent.

propositions.quote: more effective systems of detention have been developed
propositions.says: Reasons of fact: awareness of dignity after crime, a new understanding of penal sanctions, more effective systems of detention.

propositions.quote: the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person
propositions.says: The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.

matrix.why: Innocent III: the penalty can be imposed without sin under conditions. The revised 2267 on its factual reasons: today the conditions are not met. Different circumstances.

If "attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person" means that any execution is evil in its object, it denies what Innocent III required the Waldensians to profess. If "inadmissible" means "not to be admitted under present conditions", there is no conflict. The word inadmissibilis is not a term of the moral tradition and does not decide.

cases.qualifications: 1210: "not in hatred but in judgment, not incautiously but advisedly". 1995: "absolute necessity". 2018: "Today, however ... Consequently".
cases.reception: Feser and Bessette argue that the traditional teaching is irreformable and read 2267 as prudential; others (e.g., the 2018 letter's own framing as "authentic development") read it as a deeper grasp of dignity; some moralists hold it now teaches intrinsic evil. Fratelli Tutti 263–270 restates the position without settling the category.
cases.contingency: Applies to the factual reasons and passes for them. It may not be used to dissolve the dignity clause if that clause states an intrinsic moral claim (stage 6 rule).
cases.development: If the factual reading holds, what survives is the State's authority to punish in proportion and the right of legitimate defence. If the intrinsic reading holds, an earlier moral claim would be denied; the site does not count that as development.
cases.hypothesis: The revision is a moral application grounded in changed conditions and a deeper grasp of dignity, not a declaration that the penalty is intrinsically evil. (T)
cases.objection: The decisive clause gives dignity as the reason, and dignity does not change with prison systems. A penalty that attacks the inviolability of the person is wrong whenever it is inflicted, so the revision teaches that what the Church allowed for eight centuries was always wrong.
cases.rebuttal: The same paragraph introduces its conclusion with "Consequently", after factual reasons, and the Church has not called the penalty intrinsically evil in the terms Veritatis Splendor 80 uses. But the objection has textual weight that this site cannot remove, and the Holy See has not resolved it.

gaps.what: The 2018 letter of the Doctrine of the Faith
gaps.settles: Whether the Congregation frames the change as application or as a new moral norm.

gaps.what: The grade of the 1210 clause
gaps.source: The Waldensian profession in its setting; DH 795
gaps.settles: Whether it is definitive.

cases.next_source: The 2018 letter of the Doctrine of the Faith, nos. 7–8.

audio.taught: In 1210 Innocent III required converts to accept that the State may impose the death penalty without sin, if it judges justly. In 1995 John Paul II taught it should be used only in cases of absolute necessity. In 2018 the Catechism was changed to say that the death penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the dignity of the person.
audio.authority: A papal profession of faith; an encyclical; a revision of the Catechism by papal rescript. None is a solemn definition.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the dignity of the person and the State's authority to punish justly. Contingent: what penalties are necessary now. Unresolved: whether 2018 says the penalty is always wrong.

cases.title: Usury: Vix pervenit and modern interest
cases.question: Is the condemnation of usury as an injustice in the loan itself kept, or reversed, by the modern acceptance of interest?
cases.summary: Benedict XIV defined usury as taking profit from a loan by reason of the loan itself, which of its nature requires only the return of what was lent; such profit is unjust. He allowed that extrinsic titles can justify more, and that money can be invested in contracts other than lending. Lateran V had approved moderate charges by the Mountains of Piety. The principle has not been withdrawn. What changed is economic reality: when money is ordinarily productive, risk and lost opportunity become ordinary titles. The application changed under the same principle.

texts.label: Lateran V, on the Mountains of Piety (1515)

propositions.quote: from the loan itself, which of its very nature demands that only as much be returned as was received
propositions.says: Usury: profit from the loan itself, beyond the principal, by reason of the loan; all such profit is unlawful.

propositions.quote: certain other titles
propositions.says: Extrinsic titles can justly ground a demand beyond the principal; money can rightly be invested in other contracts for honest profit.
Lateran V defines that the Mountains of Piety, charging a moderate sum for expenses, are not usurious.
Lateran II condemns the rapacity of moneylenders and excludes them from ecclesiastical consolation.

matrix.why: The same encyclical: profit by reason of the loan as such is unjust; profit by reason of an extrinsic title is not. Modern interest is justified on the second ground.
A penal law against moneylenders, abrogated; the moral principle it served is kept in 1745.

cases.qualifications: "From the loan itself"; "by reason of the lending"; "titles ... not at all innate or intrinsic in general to the nature of a loan".
cases.reception: The Holy Office in the nineteenth century answered that those taking moderate legal interest were not to be disturbed (non esse inquietandos); the 1917 Code (canon 1543) allowed a legal rate where there is a just title. Some, e.g., John Noonan, read a real change of moral teaching; others read a change of fact.
cases.contingency: Passes: the economic conditions that make titles ordinary changed (H).
cases.development: What survives: a loan as such does not earn; exploitation of need is unjust.
cases.hypothesis: The principle of Vix pervenit is kept; its application changed with the nature of money and credit. (T)
cases.objection: For centuries the Church condemned charging for a loan of money in itself, not only exploitation, and modern finance charges for the loan as such; calling every interest payment an extrinsic title is a fiction that empties the principle.
cases.rebuttal: Vix pervenit itself names the titles and other contracts; what changed is how often they apply. The objection is strongest against consumer lending where no title exists beyond the loan, where the principle still bites.

gaps.what: The nineteenth-century Holy Office responses on interest
gaps.source: Collectanea S. C. de Propaganda Fide (Denzinger–Hünermann numbers to verify)
gaps.settles: How Rome applied the principle to legal interest.

audio.taught: Benedict XIV taught that it is unjust to charge for a loan just because it is a loan, but that other reasons, such as risk or lost profit, can justify a charge, and that money can be honestly invested.
audio.authority: An encyclical letter, with earlier conciliar canons and Lateran V's decree on the Mountains of Piety.
audio.permanence: Permanent: a loan as such does not earn, and exploiting need is unjust. Contingent: how often other titles apply, which changed with the economy.

cases.title: Slavery: Dum diversas, Sublimis Deus, In supremo apostolatus
cases.question: How do papal grants of servitude, papal condemnations of enslavement and the later teaching that slavery is an infamy relate: authorisation, tolerated legal status, condemnation, principle?
cases.summary: Nicholas V's Dum diversas (1452) granted the King of Portugal power to reduce Saracens and pagans to perpetual servitude. Paul III's Sublimis Deus (1537) declared that the Indians and all peoples may not be deprived of liberty or property. Gregory XVI's In supremo apostolatus (1839) condemned the slave trade. Gaudium et Spes 27 lists slavery among infamies, and Veritatis Splendor 80 lists it among acts intrinsically evil. None of the three early bulls is on the site, so the case is at the first stage. The tension is plain: a grant of perpetual servitude implies a judgment that such servitude may be imposed; the later teaching calls it intrinsically evil. Distinctions between penal servitude, just-war captivity and chattel slavery may narrow the tension, but they must be shown from the bulls, not assumed.

texts.label: Nicholas V, Dum diversas (18 June 1452) and Romanus Pontifex (1455)
Gregory XVI, In supremo apostolatus (3 December 1839)

propositions.says: Grant to the King of Portugal to invade, subdue and reduce to perpetual servitude Saracens and pagans.
propositions.note: Text not on the site; wording to be verified.
propositions.ext: Nicholas V, Dum diversas

propositions.says: The Indians and all other peoples, even outside the faith, are not to be deprived of their liberty or property, and are not to be enslaved.
propositions.ext: Paul III, Sublimis Deus

propositions.says: Condemns the trade in slaves, Black or of any race, as unworthy of the Christian name.
propositions.ext: Gregory XVI, In supremo apostolatus

propositions.quote: intrinsically evil
propositions.says: Acts by their object intrinsically evil, among which Gaudium et Spes 27 lists slavery.
propositions.note: The list itself is in GS 27 and in VS 80; check that the site's excerpts include it.

matrix.why: If Dum diversas authorises an act intrinsically evil, a papal act commanded or permitted evil; if the servitude it grants is penal servitude after a just war, a different object is at issue. Neither can be decided until the bull is read in full.
A grant of servitude over pagans against a declaration that peoples outside the faith may not be enslaved. Different addressees and circumstances; the principle in conflict is the same.

cases.qualifications: To be extracted from the bulls.
cases.reception: Panzer and Maxwell read the history in opposite directions (a consistent condemnation; a long toleration); Noonan counts slavery as a case of moral teaching that changed.
cases.contingency: Not to be applied to escape the intrinsic-evil claim (stage 6 rule). A juridical grant is abrogated; its moral premise is the question.
cases.development: Undetermined.
cases.hypothesis: None yet. The site will not propose a reconciliation before the bulls are read. (U)
cases.objection: A pope granted a king power to enslave pagans in perpetuity; the Church now teaches slavery is intrinsically evil. That is a reversal of moral judgment in papal acts.
cases.rebuttal: Not yet attempted.

gaps.what: Dum diversas and Romanus Pontifex in full
gaps.source: Bullarium patronatus Portugalliae; Davenport, European Treaties (1917)
gaps.settles: What was granted, over whom, on what ground.

gaps.what: Sublimis Deus and In supremo apostolatus
gaps.settles: The scope of each condemnation.

cases.next_source: Dum diversas in a critical edition.

audio.taught: A fifteenth-century pope allowed the King of Portugal to enslave pagans; later popes condemned enslaving peoples and the slave trade; the Second Vatican Council and John Paul II called slavery an infamy and intrinsically evil.
audio.authority: Papal bulls of different kinds; a conciliar constitution; an encyclical.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the later teaching that slavery is intrinsically evil. Unresolved: how the earlier grant relates to it. This site has not yet read the earlier bulls in full.
