cases.title: Inquisitorial law and the condemnation of torture
cases.question: Were the medieval rules allowing torture in inquisitorial procedure merely juridical, or did they assert a universal moral claim that later teaching denies?
cases.summary: Nicholas I told the Bulgarians in 866 that confessions extracted by torture are against divine and human law. Innocent IV's Ad extirpanda (1252) allowed civil authorities to use torture on heretics to extract confession, within limits. Gaudium et Spes 27 lists "torments inflicted on body or mind" among infamies, and Veritatis Splendor 80 counts physical and mental torture among acts intrinsically evil. The texts on torture are not on the site, so this case is at an early stage. As with slavery, a permission in a papal law appears to contradict a later claim of intrinsic evil; whether the permission asserted a moral proposition must be shown from its text.

texts.label: Nicholas I, Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum 86 (866)
Vatican II, Gaudium et Spes 27; John Paul II, Veritatis Splendor 80

propositions.says: Confession extracted by torture is against divine and human law; a confession must be voluntary.
propositions.ext: Nicholas I to the Bulgarians, 86

propositions.says: The podestà may compel heretics by torture, short of loss of limb or danger of death, to confess and accuse accomplices.
propositions.ext: Innocent IV, Ad extirpanda, law 25

propositions.says: Physical and mental torture are among acts intrinsically evil (citing GS 27).

matrix.why: A papal law permitting torture against a teaching that torture is intrinsically evil. If the law asserts that torture so limited is morally permissible, conflict; if it only regulated a practice of civil courts, the conflict is between a moral claim and a law, not between two moral claims. Undecided until the text is read.
Nicholas I and John Paul II reject coerced confession on the same ground.

cases.qualifications: Ad extirpanda: "citra membri diminutionem et mortis periculum" (to be verified).
cases.reception: Historians of canon law (Kuttner, Peters) treat the permission as reception of Roman procedure; moralists differ on whether a moral claim was implied.
cases.contingency: Not to be used to dissolve an intrinsic-evil claim (stage 6 rule).
cases.development: Undetermined.
cases.hypothesis: None yet. (U)
cases.objection: A pope permitted torture by law; the Church now teaches torture is intrinsically evil.
cases.rebuttal: Not yet attempted. Note that the earlier condemnation by Nicholas I shows the principle was known and taught before the permission.

gaps.what: Ad extirpanda, law 25
gaps.settles: What was permitted and on what ground.

gaps.what: Nicholas I, Responsa 86
gaps.settles: The earlier condemnation.

audio.taught: In 866 Nicholas I said that confessions forced by torture are against God's law. In 1252 Innocent IV let civil courts use limited torture on heretics. The Second Vatican Council and John Paul II taught that torture is an infamy and intrinsically evil.
audio.authority: A papal letter of guidance; a papal law, since abrogated; a conciliar constitution and an encyclical.
audio.permanence: Permanent: torture is intrinsically evil. Unresolved: whether the thirteenth-century law asserted the opposite, which this site has not yet read in full.

cases.title: Toleration or right: Mirari vos, Quanta cura, Dignitatis Humanae
cases.question: Is civil religious liberty only a contingent concession, tolerated for the common good, or a positive right?
cases.summary: Leo XIII allowed rulers to tolerate other worships for a great good or to avoid an evil; the nineteenth-century texts treat such liberty as at most a concession. Dignitatis Humanae declares a right, founded in the dignity of the person, to immunity from coercion. A right is more than a concession; so the Council says something the earlier texts did not. The question is whether it denies anything they taught. They denied a right to all manner of liberty unrestrained by any authority, grounded in indifference; the Council declares a right to immunity, limited by public order, grounded in dignity and joined to the duty toward truth. This case shares its texts with B1 and B7 and is linked to them.

texts.label: Leo XIII, Immortale Dei (1885) and Libertas (1888)

propositions.says: The Church does not condemn rulers who tolerate other worships to obtain a great good or prevent an evil.
It is by no means lawful to demand, defend or grant unconditional freedom of thought, speech, writing or worship as if these were rights given by nature.
The right to religious freedom has its foundation in the dignity of the person, known by revelation and reason, and is to become a civil right.

matrix.why: Libertas: unconditional freedom of worship is not a natural right. Dignitatis Humanae: immunity from coercion within due limits is a right founded in nature (dignity). Concord if "unconditional" and "within due limits" mark different propositions; conflict if the Council's right is the same freedom Leo denied.
Toleration answers "may the State permit?"; the right answers "may the State coerce?". The second is a further question, not the contradictory of the first.

cases.qualifications: Libertas: "unconditional"; Dignitatis Humanae: "within due limits", "immunity from coercion".
cases.reception: As B1.
cases.contingency: Partly: toleration is a prudential category; the right is not.
cases.development: The Council adds a right the nineteenth-century texts did not assert; it denies a right they did not deny only if the propositions are the same.
cases.hypothesis: Development: toleration and right answer different questions; the right the Council declares is not the unconditional freedom Leo XIII denied. (T)
cases.objection: Leo XIII denied that freedom of worship is a natural right; the Council affirms that it is. "Unconditional" is doing too much work.
cases.rebuttal: Leo's sentence denies a right to "unconditional" freedom of "thought, speech, writing or worship" as if all were equally natural rights; the Council affirms a limited immunity. The objection is strongest if the Council's "due limits" are only public order and not truth, which the Council itself does not claim to settle beyond DH 1.

gaps.what: The Latin of Libertas 42
gaps.settles: The scope of "unconditional".

audio.taught: Leo XIII said rulers may tolerate other religions for the common good, but that unconditional freedom of worship is not a natural right. The Second Vatican Council taught a natural right not to be coerced in religion, within due limits.
audio.authority: Encyclicals; a conciliar declaration.
audio.permanence: Permanent: the dignity of the person and the duty toward truth. The live question is whether the right the Council declares is the same thing Leo denied.

cases.title: Providentissimus Deus, Divino afflante Spiritu and Dei Verbum
cases.question: What is immutable about biblical inspiration and truth while methods of interpretation develop?
cases.summary: Leo XIII taught that inspiration excludes all error, not only in faith and morals, and Benedict XV rejected restricting it. Pius XII told interpreters to discern the literary forms the sacred writers used. Dei Verbum 11 teaches that the books teach "firmly, faithfully and without error that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation". Whether "for the sake of salvation" limits what is inerrant, or describes the purpose of all of it, is the open question. The Council's footnotes cite Augustine, Aquinas, Trent, Providentissimus and Divino afflante, which favours the second reading.

propositions.quote: not only excludes all error
propositions.says: Inspiration not only excludes all error but excludes it as necessarily as God cannot be the author of error.
Those err who think the historical parts depend not on the absolute truth of facts but on the opinion of the multitude.
The interpreter must discern the character, age, sources and forms of expression of the sacred writer.

propositions.quote: without error that truth which
propositions.says: The books teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth God wished put into them for the sake of our salvation.

matrix.why: Leo XIII: no error at all. Dei Verbum: without error the truth for the sake of salvation. If "for the sake of salvation" restricts the domain, a narrower claim replaces a wider one; if it describes the purpose, both say the same. The Council's notes and the relatio support the second; the text alone does not decide.
Both teach that what the writer asserts depends on his literary form; inerrancy attaches to what is asserted.

cases.qualifications: Dei Verbum 11: "everything asserted by the inspired authors must be held to be asserted by the Holy Spirit".
cases.reception: Brown and others read a restriction; Grillmeier's commentary reads purpose; the 2014 Biblical Commission document The Inspiration and Truth of Sacred Scripture discusses both.
cases.contingency: Not applicable: doctrine of inspiration. Methods are contingent; the doctrine is not.
cases.development: What survives: God is author of all Scripture; what the writers assert, the Spirit asserts; Scripture is without error in what it asserts.
cases.hypothesis: Dei Verbum describes the purpose of Scripture's truth and applies the literary-form principle of Divino afflante; it does not restrict inerrancy to salvific matters. (T)
cases.objection: The final text dropped "salutaris" as an adjective of truth only after debate, and the phrase "for the sake of our salvation" was kept precisely to qualify what is inerrant; many exegetes and some bishops took it so.
cases.rebuttal: The change from "veritas salutaris" to "veritatem quam Deus nostrae salutis causa" was made, per the relatio, to avoid the restrictive reading. That is evidence for the purpose reading; the objection is a live school dispute, not a contradiction of Leo XIII.

gaps.what: The relatio on Dei Verbum 11
gaps.settles: Why the wording was changed.

audio.taught: Leo XIII taught that Scripture, inspired by God, contains no error at all. Pius XII told scholars to pay attention to literary forms. The Second Vatican Council taught that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation.
audio.authority: Encyclicals and a dogmatic constitution.
audio.permanence: Permanent: God is the author of Scripture and it asserts no error. Developing: methods of interpretation. Debated: whether "for our salvation" limits or explains.

cases.title: Constance, Basel and Vatican I
cases.question: Can Constance's acts to end the Western Schism and the early, received acts of Basel coexist with the full, supreme, ordinary and immediate jurisdiction defined by Vatican I?
cases.summary: Constance brought three rival papal obediences together. Its acts to end the Western Schism had lasting effect. The scope and approval of Haec Sancta, especially its provision for any lawfully assembled general council, remain disputed. Martin V's final declaration approved acts done conciliariter in matters of faith without naming the decree. At Basel, session 2 protected this particular assembly. Session 3 put that claim into practice against Eugene IV. Session 11 went further: its general rule would suspend a reigning pope and transfer papal administration to the council. That rule conflicts with Lateran V and Vatican I, and the reception documents support excluding it from the acts received as binding. The case rates the limited reconciliation as plausible with medium confidence. The sources support compatibility for Constance's settlement and Basel's received acts. The claim that Haec Sancta established an independent, divinely instituted extraordinary power remains disputed.

texts.checked: The session 45 declaration is checked separately below. Gerson quotes a text on appeals attributed to Martin V. The papal instrument’s date and formal status, and Martin V’s later letters, still need checking.

texts.label: Basel, sessions 1–25 (1431–1437)
texts.edition: Summaries on the site. Session 2: COD (Tanner) I, 458; COGD II/1, 546, 548–9. Session 11: COD (Tanner) I, 466–8. Session 18: COD (Tanner) I, 458 (references from the Companion, p. 145 n. 47).
texts.checked: Tanner covers sessions 2, 3, 11, 16, 18–21, 23 and 25. The Latin of sessions 2, 3 and 11 was checked in Mansi 29. Tanner reports disagreement over the ecumenicity of sessions 1–25. Review of the remaining acts is incomplete.

texts.label: Basel, sessions 2–3: continuation of the assembly (1432)
texts.edition: Mansi 29, cols. 21–26. Session 2 at cols. 21–23. Session 3 begins at col. 23.
texts.checked: The session 2 dissolution clause names the synod of Basel. Its preceding clauses reproduce both Constance declarations. Session 3 invokes them against Eugene IV, declares his dissolution ineffective, and formally calls him to revoke it or send fully empowered representatives.

texts.label: Basel, session 11: authority of future councils (27 April 1433)
texts.edition: Mansi 29, cols. 53–55. Tanner, Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils I, pp. 466–468.
texts.checked: The Latin distinguishes the general dissolution rule and transfer of papal administration from the separate two-thirds consent rule for the present council of Basel.

texts.label: Basel, session 14: prescribed form of adherence (7 November 1433)
texts.checked: The form describes lawful continuity despite the dissolution and prescribes the terms of adherence. The surrounding decree offers, on fulfilment of its demands, to honour Eugene as head of the council.

texts.label: Eugene IV, Dudum sacrum, second form (15 December 1433), read at Basel session 16 (5 February 1434)
texts.edition: Mansi 29 (Venice, 1788; Paris reprint 1904), cols. 78–79, in the acts of Basel session 16. Also Monumenta conciliorum generalium saeculi XV 2, 565–74.
texts.checked: Checked in Mansi. The bull is dated 15 December 1433 and subscribed by cardinals. Eugene says Deus novit never issued from him or with his knowledge and revokes it as a precaution if it should appear. Session 16 approves and accepts Dudum sacrum and incorporates the revoked letters in its acts.

texts.label: Deus novit (13 September 1433), letter circulated in Eugene IV’s name
texts.edition: Printed among the letters revoked in the acts of Basel session 16, Mansi 29, cols. 82–89. See col. 86 for the disputed claim.
texts.checked: The letter calls a declaration of Basel’s lawful continuation after the dissolution sacrilegious and heretical. Publication in the acts preserves the text. Eugene’s denial of issuance leaves its status as a papal act disputed.

texts.label: Eugene IV to the Council of Basel (23 June 1434)
texts.checked: Eugene says he assented in his letters to the decree as Basel dictated it. The letter uses the singular and identifies no session 11 enactment.

texts.label: Basel after the transfer, and Florence: the "three truths" and Moyses vir Dei (1439)
texts.edition: Moyses vir Dei translated for the site from the Latin on vatican.va (COD, 2013).
texts.checked: 2026-11-18: Moyses vir Dei checked in Tanner, Florence session 7, and dated 4 September 1439 in both Tanner and the Holy See’s Latin edition: the propositions condemned "as understood in the perverse sense of the men at Basel", "contrary to the sound sense of sacred scripture, the holy fathers and the council of Constance itself"; the post-transfer acts "null ... and of no effect".

texts.label: Eugene IV and Nicholas V, 1446–1447
texts.edition: A. Mercati, Raccolta di concordati (Rome, 1919), pp. 168–170 (Ad ea ex debito, and the bull on the Basel decrees accepted by Albert II), 176 (the protest), 176–177 (Nicholas V, 28 March 1447); Mercati prints them from Raynald and Koch, collated with Reg. Vat. 365 and 380. The 1446 instructions (B13) are cited from Raynald XXVIII.
texts.checked: The 1447 bulls and protest were read against Mercati’s page images. Koch, Sylloge pp. 174–176, prints the 22 July 1446 instructions and the reservation of the power Christ gave to Peter. The Raynald witness for the 1446 text remains to be collated.

texts.label: Aeneas Silvius (1452) and Pius II, Exsecrabilis (1460)
Pius II, In minoribus agentes (26 April 1463)
texts.edition: Michael von Cotta-Schönberg, Bulls and Letters of Pope Pius II, vol. 9, preliminary edition, no. 913 (C1, fol. 116r; C2, fol. 235v).
texts.checked: Pius II honours Constance and says he knows of no approved council assembled without papal authority while an undoubted Roman pontiff reigned. The passage leaves the qualifications of any exceptional assembly open.

texts.label: Lateran V, Pastor aeternus (1516)
texts.checked: 2026-11-18: checked in Tanner, Lateran V session 11 (19 December 1516). Tanner renders the subject as "only the contemporary Roman pontiff" (pro tempore existentem: the pope reigning at the time), and the source of the right as Scripture, the Fathers, the popes, the canons and "the declarations of the same councils".

texts.label: Vatican I, Pastor aeternus (18 July 1870)
texts.edition: Holy See, Latin edition, chapters 1–4. Deferrari translation in the linked entries.
texts.checked: The Latin was read across all four chapters, including the chapter 3 canon, the prohibition of appeals to a council as a higher authority, and the conditions and irreformability of ex cathedra definitions in chapter 4.

texts.label: Jean Gerson, on appeals from the supreme pontiff in matters of faith (1418)
texts.edition: Opera omnia, ed. Louis Ellies Du Pin, vol. 2 (1706), cols. 303–304.
texts.checked: Gerson quotes and contests the prohibition attributed to Martin V, citing Haec Sancta. He says the provision was reported to have been issued on 10 March. This is a contemporary witness to the dispute. The papal instrument and its promulgation still need independent verification.

texts.label: The prosecution of Benedict XIII and Gerson’s trial materials (1417)
texts.edition: Mansi 27, cols. 1099–1100. Gerson, Opera omnia II (1706), cols. 301–302.
texts.checked: The prosecution sought removal even on an alternative that did not depend on heresy. Gerson’s trial materials distinguish conduct giving rise to suspicion from proof of heresy in Benedict’s own statements. Session 37 declared loss of office and added a precautionary deposition.

inventory.title: Basel, sessions 1–25: what each act is
inventory.note: Selected acts bearing on the seven conditions. Dates and operative clauses were checked in Tanner. For sessions 2, 3 and 11 and the second Dudum sacrum, this table also draws on the Latin in Mansi 29.

rows.act: Session 2 (15 February 1432): decree that the council was legitimately begun; inserts two declarations of Constance; no one, "even if he is distinguished by the dignity of the papacy", may dissolve, transfer or prorogue "the said synod of Basel" without its consent
rows.claim: Constitutional claim (the Constance declarations) joined to a statute of self-protection that names this council only.
rows.status: Session 2 expressly names Basel. The 1446 reception reserved the authority of the Apostolic See. The two Constance declarations inserted in this session raise a separate question about their wider scope.

rows.act: Session 3 (29 April 1432): "Impossibility of the dissolution of the council is decreed": Eugene IV's dissolution declared contrary to the decrees of Constance; the pope and cardinals summoned under penalties
rows.claim: Applies session 2 against the reigning pope.
rows.status: Basel maintained that the dissolution was legally ineffective and pressed Eugene to revoke it. His second Dudum sacrum removed the dissolution and recognised continuity on the grounds stated in the bull.

rows.act: Session 11 (27 April 1433): "For the permanent validity of the authority of general councils": a council in session cannot be dissolved or moved by a Roman pontiff without its express consent; a pope who does so and does not desist within four months is suspended by law, and after two more months the council may proceed to deprive him
rows.claim: A general law for every future council, with automatic penalties on a certain pope.
rows.status: The 1446 instructions reserved Peter’s power, and the 1447 concession for Germany reached the decrees listed at Mainz, where session 11 is absent. Its claimed general rule conflicts with Vatican I in its own terms.

rows.act: Dudum sacrum (bull dated 15 December 1433, read in session 16, 5 February 1434): Eugene IV withdraws the dissolution and declares the council lawfully continued
rows.status: The second form declares Basel lawfully continued and the earlier dissolution void. Its operative clauses recognise the council. The wider significance of that adherence remains disputed.

rows.act: Session 18 (26 June 1434): Haec Sancta renewed again and ordered published
The Compacts with the Hussites (Prague 1433; Iglau 1436)
rows.claim: Disciplinary concession of the chalice, with a doctrinal condition (Christ whole under each kind).
rows.status: Declared void by Pius II in 1462: a revocation of a contingent concession.

rows.act: Session 19 (7 September 1434): union with the Greeks; Jews and converts
rows.claim: Plans for a council of union; canonical rules.
rows.status: Superseded by events: the union was made at Ferrara–Florence.

rows.act: Sessions 20, 21 and 23 (1435–1436): reform decrees (concubinage, annates, papal election, cardinals)
rows.status: Some received in concordats (B14, B16); others lapsed or replaced.

rows.act: Session 25 (7 May 1437): the majority and minority decrees on the place of the council of union; Eugene IV transfers the council to Ferrara (18 September 1437)
rows.claim: The breaking point: the pope transfers the council without the majority's consent.
rows.status: Florence and Lateran V hold the transfer valid and void what Basel did after it (B11, 740).

outside.status: Condemned by Florence in Moyses vir Dei "according to the perverse understanding of the men of Basel" (B11). Outside sessions 1–25 and after the transfer.

outside.act: Session 34 (25 June 1439) and after: the "deposition" of Eugene IV and the election of Felix V
outside.status: Declared null by Florence (B11). Felix V abdicated in 1449 (B12).

outside.act: Session 36 (17 September 1439): the decree on the Immaculate Conception
outside.status: Without weight as an act of Basel (740); the doctrine was defined independently by Pius IX in 1854.

propositions.quote: has its power immediately from Christ
propositions.says: The synod, lawfully assembled, forming a general council and representing the Church militant, has its power immediately from Christ.
propositions.note: Formal object disputed: dogmatic decree (Küng, de Vooght), emergency measure (Jedin), or act without papal approval (classic papalist reading).

propositions.quote: even if it be papal, is bound to obey it in what pertains to the faith, to the ending of the said schism, and to the general reform
propositions.says: Everyone, even of papal dignity, must obey it in faith, the ending of the schism and reform in head and members.
propositions.note: Cerretanus (Finke II, pp. 233–234) sets the fifth session amid the negotiations to obtain John XXIII’s renunciation and records a private protest over what some expected to be passed. The account clarifies the occasion. The decree itself still lacks an express doubtful-title limitation.

propositions.quote: or of any other general council lawfully assembled
propositions.says: Contumacious refusal to obey this council, or any other general council lawfully assembled, on these matters is to be punished.
propositions.note: Tanner: "of this sacred council or of any other legitimately assembled general council". The clause reaches beyond Constance; any emergency reading must account for it (condition 6). Absent from the session-4 form.

propositions.says: Constance deposed John XXIII (Pisan) and Benedict XIII (Avignon), accepted the resignation of Gregory XII, who had first convoked it, and its electors chose Martin V.
propositions.note: Every later pope descends from this election.

propositions.says: Before the sentence, John XXIII, held at Radolfzell, promised in a signed reply to "stand by and conform to every ordinance, deliberation and determination" of the council, and, if it proceeded to remove him, to "affirm and ratify" the sentence in every way, asking only that his honour be spared; he signed: "Ego Johannes papa XXIII … approbo, confirmo ac scienter et libere volo adimplere". He declined to see the articles or to defend himself: "ipse staret iudicio concilii nec volebat alium defensorem". After the sentence of 29 May 1415, "papa sentencie acquievit et ex habundanti renunciavit in forma instrumenti inde confecti".
propositions.note: The prior reply is variously dated 25 or 28 May. Finke II, pp. 247–249, reports the council's plan to warn him that resistance could bring perpetual imprisonment. The instrument of 31 May and Fillastre's account of 1419 are separate witnesses below.
propositions.ext: John XXIII's reply at Radolfzell (late May 1415) and his acquiescence after the sentence, H. Finke, Acta Concilii Constanciensis II (Münster, 1923), pp. 40 (Fillastre) and 249–250 (Cerretanus)

propositions.says: Two days after the sentence Cossa swore to abide by it and expressly resigned any right he had or might have to the papacy.
propositions.note: The instrument records that he had time to deliberate and describes the renunciation as freely and spontaneously made. He was still detained, and the wording alone cannot settle the effect of pressure.
propositions.ext: Notarial instrument of 31 May 1415, Mansi 27, cols. 717–719

propositions.says: After gaining his liberty, Cossa personally ratified the earlier renunciation and acknowledged Martin V as the true pope.
propositions.note: Fillastre reports that Cossa initiated the submission through Florentine intermediaries. The later act gives independent support for his eventual voluntary surrender of the claim.
propositions.ext: Fillastre, in Finke, Acta Concilii Constanciensis II, pp. 169–170

propositions.says: The council, "pro tribunali sedens", "pronunciat, decernit et declarat per hanc definitivam sententiam" that Peter de Luna has been and is a perjurer, a schismatic and a heretic, "articuli fidei, Unam sanctam catholicam Ecclesiam, violatorem pertinacem", incorrigible, notorious and manifest, "a Deo ejectum & praecisum, & omni jure eidem in papatu … ipso jure privatum & ab Ecclesia catholica tanquam membrum aridum praecisum". Then, "quatenus de facto papatum … tenet", it "ad omnem cautelam privat, deponit & abjicit" him, forbids him to act as pope, and absolves all Christians from obedience to him.
propositions.note: Checked against the page image (Mansi 27, col. 1141). The form is declaratory first: the loss of office is declared as already incurred by law and by God, for pertinacious heresy against the article of faith on the one Church; the deprivation follows only "as a precaution" and only insofar as he holds the papacy in fact. He had been cited and was judged contumacious for not appearing.
propositions.ext: Constance, session 37 (26 July 1417), sentence against Peter de Luna (Benedict XIII), Mansi 27 (Venice, 1784), col. 1141; Tanner, COD, session 37

propositions.says: Frequens: general councils at fixed intervals for ever; the pope may shorten but never lengthen an interval.
propositions.note: Observed at Pavia–Siena (1423) and Basel (1431); then fell into disuse.

propositions.quote: approves all things thus done conciliarly, all things enacted in the council conciliarly concerning the matter of faith
propositions.says: Martin V approves what the council did conciliariter in matters of faith, "and not otherwise".
propositions.note: Checked in Hardt IV, cols. 1557–1558, and Mansi 27, col. 1201. The declaration answered the Falkenberg petition, which included a threatened appeal to a future council. The formula could reach beyond that case, but neither witness identifies Haec Sancta as a qualifying act. The Latin wording here is established. Its application to the decree is disputed.

propositions.says: Martin V forbids the next council to call into question what Constance "wholesomely defined" about the schism, the depositions and his own elevation.

propositions.quote: there is no authority on earth whatsoever to which one might appeal from the Roman Bishop
propositions.says: Martin V praises the King of Poland for holding that there is no appeal from the Roman Bishop.
propositions.note: The source line gives no date; the letter followed the withdrawal of the Polish appeal at Constance (1418).

propositions.says: Basel (session 2): renews Haec Sancta; this council cannot be dissolved, transferred or postponed by anyone, the pope included, without its consent.
propositions.note: Mansi 29, cols. 21–22. The dissolution clause names this synod of Basel. The immediately preceding text extends penalties for contumacy to any lawfully assembled general council on the specified matters, following Constance.

propositions.says: Basel declared Eugene IV’s dissolution ineffective under the Constance decrees. It summoned Eugene to revoke it, assist the council and attend or send fully empowered delegates.
propositions.note: The decree cites the crisis in Bohemia and the threat to reform and peace. It applied conciliar competence against a reigning pope in a dispute over this council.
propositions.ext: Basel, session 3 (29 April 1432), Mansi 29, cols. 23–26

propositions.says: Developing Frequens, the council decrees that the Roman Pontiff must attend general councils in person or by legate, whether convoked under Frequens, by Basel, "vel alterius futuri legitime congregati auctoritate"; if he neglects this, or tries in any way to hinder, move, prorogue or dissolve a council, and does not repent within four months, "extunc Romanus Pontifex a papali … administratione sint ipso facto suspensi. Quae quidem papalis administratio ad sacrum Concilium ipso jure devolvatur"; if he persists two more months, the general council proceeds against him "usque ad privationem inclusive". It further declares that a council actually assembled cannot be dissolved or moved by the Roman Pontiff without its express consent, and that the present council of Basel cannot be dissolved or moved by anyone, "etiamsi papalis fuerit dignitatis", without the consent of two thirds of each deputation.
propositions.note: Checked against the page image (Mansi 29, col. 53). The decree is general (it binds every future lawful council) and goes beyond suspension: the papal administration "devolves by law to the council". It presents itself as an interpretation of Frequens ("nullatenus prorogetur … ita prohibitive intelligi, ut etiam per Papam prorogari non possit").
propositions.ext: Basel, session 11 (27 April 1433), Mansi 29, cols. 53–55; Tanner, COD I, 466–8

propositions.says: The council prescribes to Eugene IV the text of the bull of adherence he is to issue: that the council has been lawfully continued from its beginning, the dissolution void, and that he adheres to it "pure, simpliciter & cum effectu".
propositions.note: Checked against Mansi 29, cols. 73–74 and 78–79. The bull closely follows the proposed continuation and adherence clauses while adding named cardinal consent and placing the revocations in a separate paragraph. Neither continuation clause names session 11.
propositions.ext: Basel, session 14 (7 November 1433), "Forma adhaesionis", Mansi 29, cols. 73–74

propositions.says: The letter says a general synod requires the authority of the supreme pontiff and calls a declaration that Basel lawfully continued after the dissolution sacrilegious and heretical.
propositions.note: The letter speaks in Eugene IV’s name. In Dudum sacrum he denies that it issued from him or with his knowledge and revokes it ad cautelam. Prior binding force would require proof of authentic papal issuance.
propositions.ext: Deus novit, printed in the acts of Basel session 16, Mansi 29, cols. 82–89, at col. 86

propositions.says: The bull recites that the council was lawfully begun "per Generalium Constantiensis & Senensis Conciliorum statuta, ordinationesque ... Martini Papae quinti ac nostras", and that the pope had dissolved it for causes. Because grave dissensions arose, with the consent of named cardinals, he decrees and declares that it "a tempore praedictae inchoationis suae legitime continuatum fuisse & esse ... perinde ac si nulla dissolutio facta fuisset", declares the dissolution "irritam & inanem", and adheres to the council "pure, simpliciter & cum effectu ac omni devotione & favore". He revokes two earlier bulls and, as a precaution, a third, Deus novit, which he says never issued from him or with his knowledge, and annuls whatever was done in his name "contra ejus auctoritatem".
propositions.note: Checked in Mansi 29, cols. 78–79. What the bull does not say: it states no principle that a pope cannot dissolve a council; it names neither Haec Sancta nor any decree of the council, session 11 included; it gives as its legal basis Frequens (the statutes of Constance and Siena) and the acts of Martin V and Eugene himself; and its stated reason for withdrawing the dissolution is the dissension it caused. The Companion's readings (pp. 17, 122, 251) are interpretations of this text, not its words.
propositions.ext: Eugene IV, Dudum sacrum (15 December 1433), Mansi 29, 78–90

propositions.says: Eugene IV writes that he would rather lay down the papacy and his life than be the cause by which the authority of the Apostolic See was subjected to a council against all canonical sanctions, something none of his predecessors did or was asked to do.
propositions.note: Quoted in the Companion, p. 122 n. 41. Written between the two forms of Dudum sacrum; Sigismund then pressed him to submit (p. 122).
propositions.ext: Eugene IV to the doge of Venice (late September or early October 1433), Deutsche Reichstagsakten 11, 67–8

propositions.quote: we also assented through our letters to your decree, just as you dictated
propositions.says: Eugene IV, after Dudum sacrum: he yielded and assented to the council's decree "just as you dictated", having dissented only on the place.
propositions.note: Checked against Mansi 29, cols. 579–580. The letter is dated 23 June 1434 at Florence. It confirms that the form was prescribed by Basel and leaves the wider legal reach of the adherence disputed.

propositions.says: Eugene IV transfers the council to Ferrara; the majority at Basel stays.
Basel after the transfer (session 33): conciliar superiority, and the impossibility of papal dissolution, are truths of Catholic faith; obstinate opponents are heretics.

propositions.quote: according to the perverse understanding of the men of Basel
propositions.says: Florence condemns the three propositions in the Basel sense, as contrary to the sound sense of Scripture, the Fathers "and of the council of Constance itself", and annuls Basel's acts after the transfer.
propositions.note: Checked in Tanner (Florence, session 7). The condemnation is qualified twice: by the Basel sense, and by appeal to a sound sense of Constance.

propositions.says: The king's envoys and the electors accept the decrees of Basel, with reservations for the German nation; they do not accept, "for the present", the decree suspending Eugene IV, and stand by their earlier protests on "certain other decrees". The decrees then listed are: session 1 (Frequens, under the rubric "on the authority and power of general councils"), 12, 15, 19, 20, 21, 23, 30 and 31. Session 11 is not among them; nor are sessions 2 and 18.
propositions.note: Checked against the page images (pp. 95–96). Koch (Praefatio pp. IX–XI) inserts session 2 (Sacrosancta) into his edition by inference from the rubric and from the session-31 decree Placuit divinae pietati, accepted by name, whose preamble restates Haec Sancta; he grants that the original instrument does not name it. German Wikipedia's statement that the superiority decrees were excluded goes beyond this evidence; Koch's argues the reverse for session 2. Neither touches session 11.
propositions.ext: Acceptation of Mainz (26 March 1439), C. G. Koch, Sanctio pragmatica Germanorum illustrata (Strasbourg, 1789), Sylloge pp. 95–99 (the notarial instrument); Deutsche Reichstagsakten 14, 109–14, no. 56

propositions.quote: from its beginning up to the translation made by us, without prejudice
propositions.says: Eugene IV receives Constance, and Basel from its beginning up to the translation, without prejudice to the rights of the Apostolic See and the power given by Christ to Peter.
propositions.note: Checked in C. G. Koch, Sanctio pragmatica Germanorum illustrata (Strasbourg, 1789), p. 175: "sic generalia concilia Constantiense ac Basileense ab ejus initio usque ad translationem per nos factam, absque tamen praejudicio juris, dignitatis et praeeminentiae sanctae sedis apostolicae, ac potestatis sibi et in eadem canonice sedenti in persona B. Petri a Christo concessae, cum omni reverentia et devotione suscipimus, amplectimur et veneramur." The reservation names the power given by Christ to Peter and to the one canonically seated in the See: the very power Basel's session 11 claimed to suspend. The same letter says of the decrees the German nation accepted, which the electors asked him to confirm, "cum nobis de illis non plene constet", and empowers the legates to confirm them only with compensation for the grievances some of them inflict on the Apostolic See.

propositions.says: Eugene IV receives Constance, Frequens and its other decrees "just as all other councils representing the Catholic Church militant".
propositions.note: Checked in Mercati, p. 169: "Concilium autem generale Constantiense, decretum, frequens, ac alia ejus decreta, sicut caetera alia concilia catholicam militantem Ecclesiam repraesentantia, ipsorum potestatem, authoritatem, honorem, et eminentiam ... suscipimus, amplectimur, et veneramur." Dated "MCCCCXLVI. non. februarii" (5 February 1447, modern style). The clause names Constance only; Basel is not mentioned.

propositions.says: Eugene IV allows the German nation to keep and use the decrees issued at Basel that King Albert II had accepted, with their modifications, until a legate negotiates their observance and modification or a council decides otherwise; acts done under them are confirmed. He adds that the Apostolic See is known to be gravely injured in its rights by those decrees.
propositions.note: Checked in Mercati (OCR, pp. 169–170). A concession of use for a particular nation, pending negotiation, not a reception of Basel as a council. Which decrees Albert II accepted (the Acceptation of Mainz, 1439) is still to be listed.
propositions.ext: Eugene IV, bull of 5 February 1447 on the Basel decrees accepted by Albert II, A. Mercati, Raccolta di concordati (Rome, 1919), pp. 169–170

propositions.says: The same day, Eugene IV protests that he grants the Germans' requests because necessity compels him, that he does not wish to say, confirm or concede anything against the teaching of the holy Fathers or to the prejudice of the Apostolic See, and that, being too ill to weigh everything, he holds as not answered and not granted whatever of that kind may issue from him.
propositions.note: Checked in Mercati, p. 176: "non intendimus in aliquo derogare doctrinae sanctorum patrum, aut praefatae sedis privilegiis et authoritati, habentes pro non responsis et non concessis quaecumque talia a nobis contingeret emanare."

propositions.quote: only in this one case is a certain and undoubted pope subject to a council
propositions.says: Aeneas Silvius, as papal legate: a certain pope is subject to a council only in heresy (by which he ceases to be pope), and per Haec Sancta may be deposed only for scandal to the whole Church.
Pius II condemns appeals from the Roman Pontiff to a future council as erroneous and detestable.

propositions.quote: as it was declared and defined in our age at Constance
propositions.says: Pius II recognises the authority of a general council "as it was declared and defined" at Constance, and adds that no approved council met without papal authority while there was an unquestioned pope.
propositions.note: Read in Cotta-Schönberg’s Latin edition, no. 913. Pius II qualifies his historical claim with stante Romano indubitato praesule, while an undoubted Roman pontiff held office. The statement supports a distinction between a certain pontiff and a disputed title.

propositions.quote: the Roman Pontiff alone, possessing as it were authority over all Councils, has full right and power
propositions.says: Lateran V: Basel's acts after the translation have no weight, since the Roman Pontiff alone has full right to convoke, transfer and dissolve councils.
propositions.note: Checked in Tanner: "only the contemporary Roman pontiff" (pro tempore existentem). The right belongs to the reigning pope; the text does not address a time with no certain pope.

propositions.says: Vatican I: the Roman Pontiff's jurisdiction is truly episcopal and immediate; pastors and faithful, singly and all together, owe him hierarchical subordination and true obedience in faith, morals, discipline and government.

propositions.quote: they stray from the straight path of truth who affirm that it is permitted to appeal from the judgments of the Roman Pontiffs to an ecumenical Council, as to an authority higher than the Roman Pontiff
propositions.says: Vatican I: no one may judge the judgment of the Apostolic See; appeal from the pope to a council as to a higher authority is excluded.
propositions.note: Taught in the chapter, not in the canon; the grade of the negative clause is discussed by theologians.

propositions.says: Canon: anathema to whoever denies that the Roman Pontiff has full and supreme, ordinary and immediate jurisdiction over all churches, pastors and faithful, together and singly.
Haec Sancta was adopted at Constance by the obedience of John XXIII alone, not by the whole Church, so Basel could not use it to claim supreme conciliar authority.
propositions.note: Summarised in the Companion, p. 133 (Decaluwé), who notes that the argument sits uneasily with the pope's earlier treatment of Haec Sancta as legitimate. Study: R. Bäumer, in Das Konzil von Konstanz, ed. Franzen and Müller (1964), 337–56. Cadili (p. 479 n. 19) holds that the condemnation's real object is Basel's distortion of 1439, not the Constance decree, and calls Denzinger's wider reading an error.
propositions.ext: Eugene IV, Etsi non dubitemus (21 April 1441)

matrix.why: Haec Sancta binds a person "even if papal" to obey the council in three matters; Vatican I excludes appeal from the judgments of the Roman Pontiff to a council as a higher authority. If Haec Sancta speaks of a certain pope in ordinary conditions, the two conflict. If it speaks of claimants whose title is doubtful (the situation of April 1415), they do not. The text does not say "doubtful"; the context does. Whether the context may limit the text is what condition 6 tests.

Every legitimate ecumenical council has its authority from Christ, and Vatican II teaches that the college with its head is also a subject of supreme power (LG 22). "Immediately from Christ" does not by itself deny that the pope's jurisdiction is full; conflict arises only if the council's power is taken to be over the pope as such.

Basel's statute required the consent of this council before any dissolution or transfer. Lateran V assigns the reigning pope the right to transfer or dissolve a council. The claims would conflict if Basel's consent were an inherent legal limit on the pope. Eugene IV's permission for Basel to continue supplies a narrower historical account of its practical protection in 1433.

Read in the Latin, session 11 makes a certain pope suspended by the fact itself, transfers the papal administration to the council by law, and authorises the council to proceed to deprivation. Vatican I defines that the Roman Pontiff has full, supreme, ordinary and immediate jurisdiction over all pastors and faithful, together and singly (1831). In the same sense and as universal statements of right, these contradict. The contradiction is not reconciled; it is resolved by classification: session 11 was never received by a pope (Dudum sacrum approved no decree; the 1446 reception reserved Peter's Christ-given power; the Acceptation of Mainz does not list it), and Lateran V asserts its contrary (740). The hypothesis survives only because it does not need session 11 to bind.

Session 11: no pope may dissolve or move a council in session without its consent. Lateran V: the reigning Roman pontiff alone has full right to transfer and dissolve councils. A universal negative against a universal affirmative about the same act, both as statements of right. Confirmed in the Latin (Mansi 29, col. 53): "Concilium actu congregatum dissolvi, aut de loco ad locum mutari, sine ipsius Concilii expresso consensu, per Romanum Pontificem nullatenus possit."

Read in Mansi, the bull declares a fact and a decision, not a principle: the council has been lawfully continued from its beginning, the dissolution is void, and the pope adheres to the council. It approves no decree, session 11 included, and grounds the council in Frequens and papal acts, not in Haec Sancta. Read by the textual-form rule, it does not assert that a pope cannot dissolve a council, and so does not contradict Vatican I. The conciliarist answer is serious: a pope who declares his own dissolution "void and empty" and the council lawful "as if no dissolution had been made", in words the council dictated, has in practice conceded that the dissolution lacked force; and he disowned Deus novit, the bull that stated the papal principle.

Eugene IV assented to Basel's decree in 1433–1434, then transferred the council in 1437 against the majority. Either his assent did not bind him permanently (a revocable act of government), or the transfer was unlawful. Florence and Lateran V hold the transfer lawful; the conciliarists held it unlawful.

A real contradiction, resolved by condemnation: Basel proposed conciliar superiority as a truth of faith; Florence condemned that proposition in Basel's sense. The hypothesis does not use session 33, which lies outside sessions 1–25.

Florence condemns the three truths as contrary "to the sound sense ... of the council of Constance itself". So the condemning council itself presupposes a sound sense of Constance that does not yield Basel's doctrine. What that sense is, it does not say.

Reception of Constance "just as all other councils" and a reservation of the rights of the Apostolic See, on the same day. Read together: reception qualified by the reservation. A conciliarist reads the reservation as a private protest without effect on the public act.

Pius II distinguishes councils held when a Roman pontiff was undoubted. His words are compatible with Vatican I's account of the office. He leaves open how to constitute an assembly when title is disputed and what such an assembly could decide on its own authority.

Martin V approves what was done conciliariter in matters of faith and separately forbids reopening the acts on the schism. Two different objects: the second does not depend on the first, so the depositions stand even if Haec Sancta was not approved as a matter of faith.

The texts give opposite answers about whether Basel lawfully continued during the same interval. Eugene denies that Deus novit issued from him or with his knowledge, then revokes it as a precaution. That leaves a conflict between the texts, with disputed grounds for attributing both acts to Eugene as pope.

Session 11 is absent from the Mainz list, so the 1447 concession to use the decrees Albert II accepted does not establish its reception. The broader 1446 wording and its reservation remain the other relevant evidence.

The 1446 reception covers Basel "from its beginning up to the translation", and so literally covers session 11; but it is made without prejudice to "the power given by Christ in the person of blessed Peter" to the See and to the one canonically seated in it. Session 11 subjects that same holder to suspension by law. A reception that reserves exactly the power the decree attacks does not receive the decree in that sense. The conciliarist reply is that such reservations were boilerplate and that the reception, not the reservation, was the public act.

Basel applied its asserted protection to Eugene IV. If the ruling established a jurisdictional limit on a reigning pope, it conflicts with Lateran V. The 1433 papal revocation can account for the result in practice. It does not establish the lawfulness of Basel’s original ruling.

A valid renunciation can end a title even if the council has no jurisdiction to remove a real pope. The instrument and the 1419 ratification support that route under the Pisan hypothesis. They leave the May deposition’s own authority and the exact date a valid renunciation took effect open.

cases.qualifications: Haec Sancta names three matters (faith, the ending of the schism, reform in head and members), and its penal clause reaches "any other general council lawfully assembled". Basel's session 2 speaks of "this council". Moyses vir Dei condemns the three truths in Basel's sense. Eugene IV's reception runs "up to the translation" and "without prejudice" to the Apostolic See. Medieval commentary supplies different reasons for warning or judging a pope, including notoriety and incorrigibility. Those arguments clarify the language at Constance. They leave open which of those reasons the assembly could validly apply to a legitimate pope.
cases.reception: Martin V’s recorded approval is qualified by conciliariter and matters of faith. It was given during the Falkenberg dispute, and its application to Haec Sancta remains contested. Florence invokes a sound sense of Constance when condemning Basel’s later theses. Pius II’s 1463 bull honours Constance and distinguishes cases with an undoubted Roman pontiff. That is evidence of later papal reception. It does not settle the original decree’s meaning. Scholars remain divided over the scope of Haec Sancta and the significance of Eugene IV’s adherence to Basel. See the Companion to the Council of Basel, pp. 17, 122–123, 251. Gerson’s response to the reported prohibition on appeals is contemporary evidence that he understood Haec Sancta to bind the pope in matters of faith. The scope of Martin V’s approval remains open.
cases.contingency: Several acts in this file are plainly contingent determinations and pass the test: Frequens lapsed; the Compacts were revoked by Pius II (B4); the reform decrees were partly received in concordats and partly replaced (B6, B14). The depositions are judicial acts on persons and remain settled (C11). The test does not dissolve the hard core: Haec Sancta and Basel session 2 assert a right, not only a policy, and the right asserted is constitutional.
cases.development: The limited reading preserves the four chapters of Pastor aeternus. A disputed title is a question of who holds the office instituted in the first two chapters. The full jurisdiction of its holder in chapter 3 and the conditions and irreformability of ex cathedra definitions in chapter 4 remain intact. Lumen gentium 22 describes supreme authority of the episcopal college with its head. It cannot by itself establish a headless council’s claimed competence during a schism. The Vatican I debates also distinguished the pope’s authority as head from its joint exercise with the bishops. The official report discussed hypothetical emergencies without specifying a remedy.

gate.note: Checked against the Holy See’s Latin text of Pastor aeternus. The limited reading preserves the direct institution and perpetuity of Petrine primacy, its full, supreme, ordinary and immediate jurisdiction, the rejection of appeals to a higher council and the irreformability of ex cathedra definitions.

The settlement of the schism, the election and the implementation of specific decrees demonstrate operative force. The recognition of early Basel and reception of some of its legislation are documented. The session 45 formula qualifies Martin V’s approval and leaves the reception of the constitutional clauses of Haec Sancta disputed.

The Latin confirms three distinct claims: the right asserted for Basel in session 2, the application against Eugene IV in session 3 and the general law of session 11. Dudum sacrum settled the first dissolution in practice. The 1446 reservation of Peter’s power and the Mainz list support non-reception of session 11 in its operative sense. The precise scope of the immediate Christ-derived authority claimed at Constance and Basel remains disputed.

Under protocol v0.3, divided obedience supplied an objective marker of an unresolved papal title, and the four scenarios identify who convoked the assembly in each case. The Pisan scenario now includes Cossa’s 31 May 1415 instrument and the ratification at liberty in 1419. Under the Avignon premise Benedict did not convoke the assembly. The sentence’s declaratory form and the uncertain legal premises of that declaration are assessed in the scenario below.

Frequens set a schedule that could fall into disuse. The Compacts regulated communion under both kinds and were later revoked. Florence and Lateran V declared the post-transfer acts void. These examples distinguish measures that bound for a time from acts whose claimed authority was denied.

The contemporary schism and later reception support a limited reading. Haec Sancta nevertheless extends the penal clause to any lawfully assembled general council and supplies no express doubtful-title limitation. Pius II’s reference to an undoubted pontiff is important later evidence. It leaves the decree’s original scope open. Basel session 11 is explicitly general and requires a judgment about reception.

The evidence supports the limited historical reconciliation. A conciliarist can still dispute the effect of Eugene IV’s reservations or the scope of Martin V’s approval. A defender of Vatican I can still press the Avignon scenario and the validity or effective date of Cossa’s first renunciation.

cases.hypothesis: A lawfully constituted assembly can help restore unity in a schism of rival papal titles through acts that settle the claims, obtain resignations and provide for a new election. The Roman scenario relies on Gregory XII’s convocation and resignation. The two records of Cossa’s renunciation strengthen the Pisan scenario. The Avignon scenario still depends on whether Benedict XIII already lacked title or had incurred the loss the sentence declared. In Basel’s case a reigning pope recognised the assembly and permitted its continuation. Later papal instruments received the council and certain acts with limits. The case for non-reception of session 11 is stronger than the claim that its universal rule can be harmonised with Vatican I. An immediately Christ-given, extraordinary competence in a schism remains a theological hypothesis. The concrete acts and their reception give the limited reconciliation its medium confidence. An independent and general grant of competence would require further evidence.
cases.objection: A conciliarist can point to the text of Haec Sancta: its penalties reach any lawfully assembled general council, and its obedience clause reaches papal dignity. Basel repeated both clauses, enforced them against Eugene IV and then made the central claim general in session 11. The pope accepted the council in its prescribed form and later received it up to the transfer. The objection takes that broad language as public reception of the general law despite the reservation. A defender of Vatican I can ask what legally authorised the April 1415 assembly under the Roman or Avignon account. He can also ask what gave it authority to declare Benedict XIII already deprived, or whether Cossa’s detention impaired his 1415 consent. The fact that condition 4 was reworded after an earlier failure is recorded alongside the earlier verdict.
cases.rebuttal: Martin V’s declaration supports a qualified reading of reception. The application to Haec Sancta is uncertain because the declaration does not name it. The 1433 Basel bull makes the dissolution void for this assembly. Its operative clauses do not enact session 11’s rule. The explicit reservation of Peter’s power in the 1446 instructions and the absence of session 11 from Mainz provide separate reasons for reading the later reception as limited. Constance’s record supports several mechanisms for settling the schism. Cossa swore and expressly resigned in 1415, then reaffirmed the resignation at liberty in 1419. The latter act strengthens the eventual surrender under the Pisan premise. It cannot establish whether the May 1415 sentence took effect immediately. The Avignon sentence states a prior loss of office and adds a precautionary deposition. Its declaratory form is established. Its legal and theological premises remain disputed. These limits account for the provisional verdict. The proposed Romanus pontifex procedure at Constance helps explain what some reformers thought an emergency might require. Its abandonment leaves the acts against individual claimants and the general authority to judge a reigning pope as distinct questions. Sutri’s conflicting witness accounts likewise leave the basis of the settlement open.

cases.benedict: Inference from Benedict's method: a council is not a constituent assembly that can replace the Church's constitution (rule 1). Read that way, Constance did not create a new constitution but restored the existing one to a certain head; Basel, when it claimed to make conciliar superiority a dogma, attempted what the rule forbids. This is the site's application, not Benedict XVI's judgment on Constance or Basel.

audio.taught: Constance said that its power came directly from Christ and claimed obedience even from someone of papal dignity. Basel protected this assembly in session 2. In session 11 it claimed a general power to suspend a pope and take over papal administration. Vatican I defined the pope’s full and supreme jurisdiction and rejected appeals to a council as a higher authority.
audio.authority: Vatican I defined the primacy. Constance’s settlement of the schism had lasting effect. Martin V’s final declaration supports qualified reception, while the reception of Haec Sancta itself remains disputed. The 1446 reservation and the list of Basel decrees accepted at Mainz support the exclusion of session 11 from the received law.
audio.permanence: The primacy defined at Vatican I is permanent. Practical arrangements such as the schedule of councils could change. The evidence gives medium confidence that the acts settling the schism and the received acts of Basel can be reconciled with Vatican I. The wider thesis about extraordinary conciliar authority remains disputed.

counterfactuals.title: Which line was the true papacy? The case under each answer
counterfactuals.note: Condition 4 (v0.3) requires the historical case to be tested under each rival account of the legitimate papal line, because who convoked Constance, and with what authority, depends on it. The Church has not defined which line was legitimate. The Annuario Pontificio, since the list revised for it in the mid-twentieth century, counts the Roman line (Gregory XII) as legitimate and the Pisan and Avignon claimants as antipopes; Angelo Roncalli took the name John XXIII in 1958. That listing is a historical judgment, not a definition (P3). Martin V, in his own register, called the Pisan Alexander V "our predecessor" (C10).
counterfactuals.common: One result holds under every scenario. Martin V, elected on 11 November 1417, was received by the whole Church, including the last Spanish obediences. The classical theologians (John of St Thomas, Billot) hold that the peaceful acceptance of a pope by the universal Church is a certain sign of his legitimate title, a dogmatic fact. So the succession from 1417 is certain whichever line was true, and does not depend on Haec Sancta. (T)

rows.label: The Roman line was legitimate (Gregory XII)
rows.support: The Annuario Pontificio's present list; the resignation was received at session 14 as a pope's; Gill, Brandmüller and the classical papalist reading. (H, T)
rows.convocation: Gregory XII authorised the assembly through his legates in session 14 (4 July 1415), before resigning. Under this premise the initial summons came from a claimant without papal title.
rows.haec_sancta: Passed at session 5 (6 April 1415), before the legitimate convocation: on this premise not an act of an ecumenical council. It binds, if at all, only through later reception (Martin V's conciliariter approval, C9; the 1446 reception "from its beginning", saving Peter's power).
rows.depositions: John XXIII was not pope, so his deposition judged no pope. Benedict XIII was not pope. Gregory XII resigned freely. The see was vacant from 4 July 1415, and the council acted in a vacancy.
rows.needs_extraordinary: No. The ordinary constitution suffices: a true pope convoked and resigned; the council governed during a vacancy and provided for an election.
rows.conditions: Condition 4 passes easily (a legitimate pope convoked). Condition 2 is weakest here: Haec Sancta has no conciliar authority of its own. The hypothesis is consistent with Vatican I but is not needed.

rows.label: The Pisan line was legitimate (Alexander V, John XXIII)
rows.support: Martin V's own register ("Alexander papa V predecessor noster", C10) and his description of John XXIII's deposition as "canonical" (C8); the larger obedience in 1414; the Council of Pisa's claim to have deposed both other claimants in 1409. (H)
rows.convocation: Legitimate from the start: John XXIII, the true pope on this premise, convoked Constance (at Sigismund's urging).
rows.haec_sancta: Passed by a legitimately convoked council after its pope had fled (20–21 March 1415), and without his approval. On the classical rule it binds only as far as a pope later approved it (Martin V, conciliariter, C9).
rows.depositions: Constance sentenced John XXIII on 29 May 1415. On 31 May he ratified the sentence, swore to abide by it and expressly renounced his rights (Mansi 27, cols. 717–719). Fillastre reports that he renewed that renunciation in 1419 after gaining his liberty (Finke II, pp. 169–170).
rows.needs_extraordinary: A valid renunciation can account for the eventual surrender without a jurisdiction to depose a true pope. The 1415 instrument records freedom of consent while he was detained. The independent, later ratification supports eventual voluntary surrender without determining when the first act took effect.
rows.conditions: The Pisan pope convoked the assembly on this premise. The two renunciation records bear on the effect of the sentence. The timing and effect of possible coercion in 1415 remain open.

rows.label: The Avignon line was legitimate (Benedict XIII)
rows.support: Aragon, Castile, Navarre and Scotland held to it until 1415–1416; Benedict never resigned. Few modern historians defend it. (H)
rows.convocation: Never by the true pope: Benedict XIII rejected Constance. The council's authority over him would have to come from elsewhere.
rows.haec_sancta: An act of an assembly that, on this premise, had no legitimate convocation; it binds only through later papal reception.
rows.depositions: The council deposed, on this premise, the true pope, against his will (session 37, 26 July 1417), after the Capitulation of Narbonne had withdrawn his last kingdoms. But the sentence (Mansi 27, col. 1141; checked) is declaratory in form: it declares him a pertinacious heretic against the article of faith "one holy catholic Church", "cast out and cut off by God" and "deprived by the law itself" of every right in the papacy; only then, as a precaution and insofar as he holds the papacy in fact, does it deprive and depose him.
rows.needs_extraordinary: The sentence’s declaration of a previous loss of office resembles Bellarmine’s later view that manifest heresy itself causes the loss. Cajetan held that an act of deposition was required. The prosecutors also argued for removal even without heresy, a ground distinct from the sentence’s declaration. Under the Avignon premise the questions are whether Benedict was a manifest, pertinacious heretic, what took away his title, and who could make that judgment.
rows.conditions: Condition 4 assesses the divided obediences and the source of convocation under v0.3. The Avignon premise leaves jurisdiction and the legal effect of the sentence open, including the alleged grounds for prior loss of office.

rows.label: No claimant was certainly pope (papa dubius)
rows.support: The canonists' maxim "papa dubius, papa nullus"; the hypothesis itself; Jedin's reading of Haec Sancta as an emergency measure. (T)
rows.convocation: By a claimant (John XXIII) with the emperor, then confirmed by a second claimant's convocation (Gregory XII, session 14). No convocation by a certain pope was possible.
rows.haec_sancta: An act of the only body that could restore a certain head; binding in that emergency sense, received later saving Peter's power.
rows.depositions: The council judged claimants, none of them certainly pope; no certain pope was judged.
rows.needs_extraordinary: Yes, and only in this limited form: authority to settle a doubtful title, not authority over a certain pope.
rows.conditions: Condition 4 is met in the sense the hypothesis needs: the criterion is objective (no peaceful acceptance) and cannot be invoked against a certain pope.

counterfactuals.result: Under the Roman premise the convocation and resignation of Gregory XII provide a path through the ordinary constitution. Under the Pisan premise two records support Cossa’s eventual renunciation. Under the Avignon premise the sentence states a previous loss of office, whose legal grounds remain contested. Under the doubtful-title premise, restorative competence is a plausible explanation of how Constance settled rival claims.

verdict_history.why: Condition 4 failed under its v0.2 wording; a failed condition means unresolved.
No condition fails under v0.3: 1, 4 and 5 pass; 2, 3, 6 and 7 are partly met. The rubric allows plausible concord, with live objections stated.

The notarial instrument and the 1419 witness strengthen the Pisan account. The Basel Latin and reception instruments support a distinction between acts for this council and session 11’s general law. The verified wording of Martin V and Pius II supports the qualified reading, while Haec Sancta’s reception and the Avignon premise keep the result provisional.

The new review distinguishes evidence that historical actors proposed an emergency theory from evidence that the Church enacted or received it. The limited reconciliation remains plausible. The broader claim about judging a pope for notorious, incorrigible scandal still requires independent proof.

Deus novit and Dudum sacrum disagree about Basel’s continuation. Checking the letter, the revocation and Segovia clarifies which claims have documentary support and which require proof of authorisation or formal synodal action.
